items.title: Iran Microwaves Babies! Rep Joe Wilson Concocts Bizarre Justification For Iran War
items.content_text:
Iran Microwaves Babies! Rep Joe Wilson Concocts Bizarre Justification For Iran War

This is a new one, and quite insane in terms of pro-war propaganda coming from elected officials...

South Carolina Rep. Joe Wilson (R) has bizarrely claimed that Iranians have been putting babies in microwaves. This was his response when pressed this week to offer a justification for the Iran war by independent journalist and longtime Middle East regional pundit Rania Khalek.

Khalek walked with him through Congressional halls and peppered him with questions highlighting the unpopularity of the Iran war among the American public.

Ironically, Rep. Wilson barely won his reelection campaign by an incresibly slim 0.95 points - and he was up against a 25-year-old Democratic challenger and first-time candidate.

"I oppose terrorists who murder babies by putting them in microwaves," Wilson asserted, and also presented as 'evidence' his own eyewitness experience, supposedly on the ground while on a visit to Iran.

Here's the transcript of the exchange via "Useful Idiots" podcast:

Rania Khalek: Do you support continuing funding the war on Iran when 74% of voters said that it was a crucial part of their decision to–

Rep. Joe Wilson: I oppose terrorists who murder babies by putting them in microwaves.

Rania Khalek: I’m sorry, who put babies in microwaves? Where did you hear this? I’ve seen no evidence.

Rep. Joe Wilson: I’ve visited Iran.

Wilson quickly brushed off and showed no concern for the Minab school bombing and massacre when he was presented with the immense death toll of Iranian children, young girls, and teachers. He dismissed it as "propaganda".

It should be noted that there is zero documention of Wilson ever having visited Iran. What's more is he didn't just claim to have gone to the Islamic Republic - but is suggesting that while there he uncovered evidence of babies being microwaved.

This whole encounter between Wilson and Khalek rivals or perhaps even surpasses the incubator babies hoax that was used to sell the first US invasion of Iraq (in 1991).

For a trip down memory lane...

Three months after Nayirah testified, President George H.W. Bush launched the invasion of Iraq. But it turned out Nayirah’s claims weren’t true. No human rights group or news outlet could confirm what she said. It also turned out Nayirah was not just any Kuwaiti teenager. She was the daughter of the Kuwaiti ambassador to the United States, Saud Nasser al-Sabah. She had been coached by the public relations firm Hill & Knowlton, which was working for the Kuwaiti government.

"They took the babies out of the incubabors... and left the babies to die on the cold floor".

Americans are some of the most propagandized people on earth, and often this translates to disastrous 'shock and awe' style consequences for nations in Washington's immediate crosshairs. This often results in a domino effect of so-called 'unintended consquences' and the dire suffering of entire populations and regions.

items.title: Net Zero Is Falling Apart, One Target At A Time
items.content_text:
Net Zero Is Falling Apart, One Target At A Time

Authored by Ross Clark via CapX,

This week it seems that another Net Zero domino will fall. The British Government is reported to be on the point of announcing that the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which lays down targets for the sale of new cars, will be watered down. This follows a consultation launched in August. At present, manufacturers are under an obligation to ensure that a rising percentage of their vehicles are pure electric or else face punitive fines of up to £12,000 for every petrol and diesel vehicle they sell over the limit. The required proportion rises from 33 percent in 2026 to 80 percent in 2030 and thereafter to 100 percent by 2035, at which point even hybrids will be banned. The UK car industry is falling well short of the targets, in spite of offering large incentives on electric vehicles. 26.6 percent of new cars sold in Britain so far this year have been pure electric. The industry also fell short of the 22 percent and 28 percent targets in 2024 and 2025 but largely avoided fines because of get-out clauses which made some allowance for increased hybrid sales.

Actually, the situation for UK manufacturers is more dire than the above figures suggest. A growing share of electric vehicle sales are coming from Chinese manufacturers who are able to undercut European ones, thanks in part to China's dominance in battery manufacturing. Jaecoo accounted for 1.2 percent of the UK market in 2025 and 3.4 percent so far in 2026. BYD increased its market share from 2.3 percent to 3.9 percent over the same period. In other words, European manufacturers are falling shorter of the ZEV target than the overall figures suggest. It is becoming painfully clear that a continuation of the ZEV mandate on its current trajectory is going to cause further serious damage, if not deliver a fatal blow to UK car manufacturing. Some ministers, including Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, are said to favor reducing the 2030 target to 50 percent.

Unsurprisingly, Labour's Net Zero fundamentalists such as Ed Miliband are reported to be against reducing the target. But the issue is complicated by Andy Burnham's negotiations for a reset of Britain's relations with the EU. Electric vehicles represent one area in which UK regulation, post-Brexit, has been more stringent than EU regulation. EU rules already allow for a small proportion of cars manufactured after 2035 to have internal combustion engines. The European Parliament's Environment Committee last week voted for a further relaxation. If Burnham signs up for a deal which forces Britain into "dynamic alignment" with EU regulations, it will almost certainly mean us having to adopt the same EV targets as the EU. Labour ministers who are both Europhile and Net Zero fundamentalists are going to have to choose what is most important to them.

But there is something even more significant to be drawn from the revision of ZEV targets. Virtually every interim target on the way to the Government's overall, legally binding 2050 Net Zero target is being abandoned, or relaxed, as it flies headlong into reality. New oil-fired boilers were due to be banned from 2026, gas-fired boilers by 2035. There were going to be 600,000 heat pump installations a year by 2028.

All these targets have gone, once it became clear that they could not be met. Moreover, the electricity grid was going to be fully decarbonized by 2030; that target has already been subtly downgraded to 95 percent carbon-free and is coming under constant pressure. Another target soon to go will likely be the one requiring 10 percent of jet fuel used by airlines to be Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) by 2030. The Government confirmed this target last month, but as with ZEV, the use of SAF is running well behind track.

Yet at the same time the Government continues to insist that it remains committed to its overall Net Zero target of 2050. But how does it expect to be able to achieve that when it is on a trajectory well short of what it used to think was necessary to achieve this? The year 2050, perhaps, still lies such a distance into the future that the current generation of ministers and MPs feel they don't need to worry about it too much. At some point, though, the 2050 Net Zero target is going to reach a crunch point at which it has to be relaxed, if not abandoned altogether. I doubt the current Government will want to make the call, but I will give the 2050 Net Zero target until 2030 at the latest.

items.title: White House Confirms Unprecedented Trump-Xi-Putin Trilateral Summit: Nukes In, Ukraine Out
items.content_text:
White House Confirms Unprecedented Trump-Xi-Putin Trilateral Summit: Nukes In, Ukraine Out

President Trump will sit down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday, the White House said Friday, in what US officials described as the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers. 

According to the NY Post, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters on a call Friday evening that "President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting" on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which China hosts Nov. 18-19. "The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world," Wales said. "This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous."

Officials said they do not expect the leaders to reach any concrete agreement, describing the sit-down as an initial conversation, and Trump and Putin will not hold a separate one-on-one meeting, officials told reporters.

Trump previewed the meeting on Nov. 8, speaking to reporters before flying back to Washington from Florida: "One of the meetings, I think, will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be interesting. We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization," he said, adding: "We're trying to end the war in Iran."

.@POTUS: "I'm going to be going to China... One of the meetings, I think, will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be interesting. We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization." pic.twitter.com/X03kk6DJpB

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 9, 2026

For Trump, the summit is a chance to pitch something he's talked about for years. "There's no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many," he said in the Oval Office in February 2025. "You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over." His proposal for the US, China and Russia then: "Let's cut our military budget in half."

New START, the last treaty capping US and Russian strategic arsenals, lapsed on Feb. 5 without a replacement, and as we reported at the time, the two countries now have no limits on their nuclear weapons for the first time in decades.

Trump had said in January that "I think it would be appropriate for the Chinese" to be part of any replacement. Beijing answered the day after the treaty lapsed: "China will not take part in nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage," said Shen Jian, its ambassador for disarmament affairs, adding that Washington and Moscow have "special and primary responsibilities" to cut their arsenals first, Arms Control Today reported.

A senior US official said Trump also intends to raise his war with Iran with both leaders: "I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin."

Officials said Washington runs a separate negotiating track on Ukraine with Kyiv and Moscow. "China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," a second official said.

The three-way meeting was Putin's idea: as we noted last month, he floated it in an Oct. 9 call with Trump as a venue to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war, with Zelensky not invited, and the Kremlin pointed to the APEC sidelines in Shenzhen. Trump said he "would do it" if Xi was on board, and steered it toward denuclearization. Within days, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said China was already preparing it, and on Oct. 25 he said that "Moscow, Beijing, and Washington are in principle ready to hold it."

According to the White House's version, Trump isn't planning to discuss the war in Ukraine. Moscow, however, describes it differently: on Nov. 12, a day before the White House briefing, Ushakov told reporters that Putin would take up the settlement of the war with Trump when the two meet in Shenzhen: "we will continue to discuss the full range of issues related to the settlement," he said, according to RIA Novosti.

Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow this week, where Ushakov rebuffed Washington's push to bring the Europeans to the table, after the latest round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Nov. 3 that "work is under way on organising such a meeting." Three days later, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China "is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state," the first time Beijing confirmed the talks.

Analysts the AP spoke to doubt it will go further than the photo. "China wants the image but not the costs," said Sun Yun of the Stimson Center. Craig Singleton put it more bluntly: "The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential."

Trump also has a working lunch and a bilateral meeting with Xi on Thursday, their fourth meeting since Trump returned to the White House, on his second trip to China this year, with a trade truce that runs out in January hanging over it. China this week extended its pause on rare earth export controls to Jan. 10, though, as we noted, the metal squeezing buyers hardest was never covered by it.

Chip curbs aren't on the table: "We do not negotiate American export controls," the second official said, days after Beijing accused Washington of using the Nvidia spy scandal to justify a chip "blockade." Officials also don't expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the Chinese tech executive accused of spying whose alleged affair with Jensen Huang preceded his exit as Nvidia's CEO, which we have covered.

Trump leaves Washington on Monday for the ASEAN summit in Manila before flying on to Shenzhen. Elon Musk will travel with him but will not take part in the meeting with Xi and Putin, officials said.

When they meet Thursday, the three men who control the bulk of the world's nuclear warheads will sit at one table with no treaty left between any of them.

items.title: Who Whacked Jensen Huang? The CIA Wasn't Convinced - So Rubio Reworked Their Memo
items.content_text:
Who Whacked Jensen Huang? The CIA Wasn't Convinced - So Rubio Reworked Their Memo

The classified memo whose leak set off Jensen Huang's fall at Nvidia was Marco Rubio's work, and Rubio built it from a CIA report that he recast "in his own more assertive terms," according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke to the Washington Post for a report published Friday.

According to the report, CIA officials are "not yet convinced" that the intelligence gathered on Alice Huang - including intercepted communications - show she was knowingly passing information to Beijing, a source told CNN. Some officials at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence have called the spy label "over-torqued," according to the network, while others say her access to Huang, and through him to President Trump, made her a counterintelligence risk whether or not she ever passed anything on.

The memo, overseen by Rubio as secretary of state and national security adviser, went to senior officials in the spring, before Trump's May trip to Beijing, and Rubio also warned Trump in person, as we reported. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nov. 12 that neither the Justice Department nor the FBI has confirmed whether Alice Huang was a spy, as we noted. Beijing denies it.

Commentator Arnaud Bertrand put the two reports side by side: if the CIA's own analysts weren't convinced, the "spy" framing was Rubio's, not the agency's.

Interesting: the Washington Post says that Jensen Huang's downfall was Marco Rubio's doing (https://t.co/3rtFza8rje), and it looks like the "spy" framing was directly his and not the CIA's.

As they write, Rubio took a CIA report and rewrote it in a memo "in his own more... https://t.co/hiJ8UOAvWW pic.twitter.com/cQ5mJR1sLE

— Arnaud Bertrand (@RnaudBertrand) November 14, 2026

A shadow war for Trump's ear

According to the Post, the entire affair was the climax of a long fight over who sets Trump's China policy. Huang won unusual access to the president and approval to sell AI chips to China, and China hawks across both parties, in the administration, Congress and the think tanks, had spent years trying to break that hold. "They wanted to destroy the influence Jensen had over the president," one former official told the paper, which called Huang's exit a major win for that camp.

At the G7 in Paris, Rubio repeatedly declined to discuss his role. Asked whether the allegations changed his view of AI talks with Beijing, he said, "I work for the American people."

Three bipartisan chip bills are now riding in the Senate's version of the annual defense bill: the AI Overwatch Act from Sens. Jim Banks and Elizabeth Warren, which would give Congress power over chip export licenses, the Chip Security Act, aimed at smuggling, and Sen. Pete Ricketts' MATCH Act, which would press allies to stop selling chipmaking tools to China, the South China Morning Post reported Nov. 11. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he would work to "make sure that those provisions make it into the final version."

The open-weights theory

Huang was also Washington's loudest corporate defender of open-weight AI: his first-ever X post, in July, was a letter arguing that open models are essential to American AI leadership, as we detailed. Physicist and investor Steve Hsu wrote that he had heard "on very good authority" that Nvidia was planning "to go hard at producing frontier class open models", so as not to depend on OpenAI or Anthropic to drive the industry forward.

In the past months I heard on very good authority that Jensen and Nvidia were planning to go hard at producing frontier class open models. 

They wanted to verticalize their AI presence, and not depend on OAI or ANT to drive the industry forward.

OAI, ANT, and GOOG are...

— steve hsu (@hsu_steve) November 12, 2026

Glenn Greenwald put the suspicion bluntly: "I don't know who wanted Jensen Huang out but I know that whoever it was wields extreme levels of power."

I don't know who wanted Jensen Huang out but I know that whoever it was wields extreme levels of power.

Nobody actually believes that, in the age of Donald J. Trump, very powerful people rapidly fall due to extramarital affairs, right? Even if accompanied by anonymous... https://t.co/4KyW338eoF

— Glenn Greenwald (@ggreenwald) November 12, 2026

The tip from inside tech

The New York Times investigation that first tied Huang to Alice Huang also started outside government. Times reporter Tripp Mickle said on the paper's The Daily podcast on Nov. 10 that he and Ana Swanson got a message last August from "a tech industry contact" telling them to "drop everything and look at this company called Megaspeed." He did not name the contact.

Megaspeed is the Singapore-based renter of Nvidia computing power where Alice Huang once worked. That same August, Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter emailed the Commerce Department agents building a chip-smuggling case against Megaspeed, after which Commerce paused its work and the case moved to the Justice Department, as we reported. Nvidia has said it contacts officials to "answer their questions."

Others went straight for Anthropic's Dario Amodei, a leading advocate of tight AI rules and chip export limits. "Dario might be behind this whole Jensen Huang thing," read one widely shared post, pointing to the $40 million Anthropic has given Public First Action, a group pushing for AI safeguards and export controls. Anthropic has said those gifts cannot be used to influence any election.

Dario might be behind this whole Jensen Huang thing.

Anthropic donated $40M to PublicFirstAction, which was founded by former U.S. Representative Brad Carson and Chris Stewart to advocate for AI safeguards and chip export controls.

Representative Brian Mast is leading the... pic.twitter.com/tWlnidNGtq

— Jinjing Liang (@JinjingLiang) November 12, 2026

A viral Chinese-language post went further and named an Anthropic co-founder as the Times' tipster, citing only "open-source intelligence"; Mickle named no one. Nvidia, meanwhile, committed $10 billion to the private placement alongside Anthropic's IPO, according to Anthropic's amended filing, making Huang's company one of the biggest buyers of the rival that supposedly knifed him.

Singapore pushes back

Researcher Brian Chau went after the Wall Street Journal, who pointed out the outlet's correction noting that they fabricated statements from the Singapore government regarding an alleged investigation into Alice Huang.

Today's Jensen Update Thread

1. WSJ fabricated statements from the Singapore government pic.twitter.com/irgIDi7yot

— Brian Chau (@brianchau57) November 14, 2026

Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs had already disputed the Journal's Oct. 30 report that Singapore officials had concerns about Alice Huang's ties to Huang and to Chinese intelligence. "Neither the Singapore Government nor its officials said this," the ministry said Oct. 31, adding that its reply to the paper never mentioned her and only confirmed that the police investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing.

What's left

Huang admitted he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, reports of further relationships followed, including one with a subordinate, and on Nov. 11 Nvidia's board accepted his resignation "effective immediately", according to the company's 8-K, which gives no reason. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair.

Prediction markets have other ideas: Arm CEO Rene Haas, Huang's onetime protege, became the favorite on Polymarket after the board approached him on Friday. Elon Musk, on the prospect of bringing Huang on, posted in response to us:

That would be an honor

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 12, 2026

Beijing says Washington is using the scandal to justify a chip "blockade." The stock closed at $166.19 on Nov. 12, the day the resignation was announced, down 4.34% on the day and about 31% below its Oct. 6 record close of $239.24.

Whoever pulled the trigger, Nvidia reports quarterly results on Nov. 17 without Huang in the room, while the hawks' three chip bills ride toward the final defense bill.

items.title: Donbas For NATO? Zelensky Says Washington Just Floated A Swap That Crosses Putin's Reddest Line
items.content_text:
Donbas For NATO? Zelensky Says Washington Just Floated A Swap That Crosses Putin's Reddest Line

Volodymyr Zelensky says US negotiators asked for the first time whether Ukraine would pull out of Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, a trade that would hand Moscow the land it has demanded for years while putting Kyiv inside the alliance Vladimir Putin calls a red line.

"The Americans raised the question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'" Zelensky told journalists, according to the Kyiv Independent. 

"This was the first time this issue had been raised."

The question came out of two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, which ended without a breakthrough but with a deal to swap more than 1,000 prisoners, as we reported. Final numbers for the exchange were still under discussion, according to Reuters.

Zelensky said Kyiv is not ready to give up territory, but he would put the question to a national referendum if Ukraine got a full package: security guarantees, a strong and funded army, and money to rebuild. "If the American side confirms this to us together with other NATO colleagues, then I will ask the opinion of our society," he said, per the Kyiv Post. "I have no right to make that decision on my own."

He drew one line in advance: any deal would come "without any recognition of the occupied territories as Russian." He wants guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5 "as an absolute minimum," and said Washington told him no US soldiers would deploy to Ukrainian soil.

"But we need specifics, and we don't have them yet. All of this is still under discussion," Zelensky said.

 NATO "is back on the agenda," he added, but Putin's signals point to "an extremely difficult conversation."

The opening would reverse Washington's line, since US officials had previously said Ukrainian NATO membership was off the table. It also follows a rough stretch between Kyiv and the White House, with Trump pressing Ukraine to pause strikes on Russian oil facilities while his waiver let Russian diesel exports double, and Zelensky complaining again about Starshield disruptions.

Putin has long called Ukrainian NATO membership a red line and cited it as one reason for the 2022 invasion. Zelensky made clear he expects no give from Moscow on the map either. "When Putin says something about state borders, it is certainly not about reducing Russia's territory, right?" he said. "Therefore, there is no faith in the comrade in the Kremlin."

He also dismissed Putin's offer of a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a contested city in the Donetsk region, as proof Russia can't take it by force. "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way," Zelensky said, according to RTE. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised an energy ceasefire with Putin in Moscow on Thursday with no reported progress, and Zelensky said "Putin personally does not support a ceasefire."

Zelensky met Witkoff and Kushner outside Dublin on Thursday and said the US side told him all parties had agreed Europe would get a seat at the next round, the result Kushner went all in on after Putin aide Yuri Ushakov poured cold water on the idea. EU leaders meeting in Dublin agreed Europe's team would be Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, plus the bloc's institutions.

The NATO question follows a plan Kyiv turned down days earlier. Trump's envoys proposed redrawing the administrative borders of Donetsk and Luhansk along the current front line, which would let Moscow claim all of Donbas without capturing the Ukrainian-held cities it still wants, according to The Telegraph. A Ukrainian source told the paper Kyiv would never recognize it, de facto or de jure.

Zelensky has described a US Donbas-for-security link before. In March he told Reuters Washington would finalize security guarantees "once Ukraine is ready to withdraw from Donbas," as we noted. Secretary of State Marco Rubio shot that down two days later: "he knows that's not true."

items.title: Travel Hell Continues: 1000s Still Stranded After Ground Stop As Duffy Demands $50 Billion: 'This Is An Emergency'
items.content_text:
Travel Hell Continues: 1000s Still Stranded After Ground Stop As Duffy Demands $50 Billion: 'This Is An Emergency'

More than 3,000 flights within, into or out of the US had been canceled by Saturday morning, according to FlightAware, as airlines dug out from Friday's nationwide ground stop, which wiped out more than 9,100 flights that day and left tens of thousands of passengers stuck in airports overnight.

As we reported Friday night, the FAA lifted the stop at about 8:15 p.m. ET, roughly four hours after it halted every departure in the country. It was only the second nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks; the first came in January 2023, when the FAA's pilot-alert system failed.

The safety of the flying public is always the FAA's highest priority. The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming. Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable....

— The FAA ✈️ (@FAANews) November 14, 2026

"It's going to be slow," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters at the White House Friday night, warning that airlines would need time to get back to normal capacity and that some passengers would have to be rebooked.

"Nickel And Diming It"

Duffy said the trouble began at 3:36 p.m., when the FAA saw "instability for our radar and our communications" at centers across the country, according to the transcript of the briefing. "Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," he said, adding that the FAA's new IP switches stayed up: "it's the old hardware that went down." Elsewhere in the briefing he said, "We use 1980s little copper lines."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin offered a less flattering version for the modernization effort itself: the new equipment the FAA has been bolting onto the network "was overwhelming the older system." Piecing the upgrade together, he said, is the problem: "nickel and diming it together does not work."

On Thursday, a day before the outage, Duffy and budget director Russ Vought sent appropriators a letter asking for $30.1 billion, Roll Call reported, a request that mirrors the Modern Skies Act Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) introduced in September; only $10.1 billion of that bill goes to air traffic control upgrades.

By Friday night the ask was $50 billion. "This is an emergency -- I want Congress to give us emergency funding," Duffy said. "I want $50 billion." Mullin put a "complete overhaul" at about the same figure. That is $19.9 billion more than the White House had put in writing the day before.

Today's nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD, analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century.⁰@FAANews is modernizing this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down... pic.twitter.com/nXUPHkdNdV

— Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 14, 2026

Congress already gave the FAA $12.5 billion in the July 2025 reconciliation law, which Duffy called partial funding. In January, as we noted, the FAA put the whole overhaul at "at least $32.5 billion" and Duffy was asking Congress for another $20 billion to finish it by the end of Trump's term. Thursday's letter alone, on top of the $12.5 billion, put the total at $42.6 billion, more than $10 billion above that estimate, before Friday's number pushed it higher still.

"We're Looking At That"

Mullin said investigators had found no sign of a cyberattack. "There's no chatter," he said. "We haven't seen any footprints, as you would say, or identifications of people that got into the system."

Asked whether the FAA's new AI traffic tool had anything to do with it, Mullin didn't rule it out:

REPORTER: "There are reports that the FAA was rolling out a new A.I. traffic control system today. Has there been any link between that?"

SEC. MULLIN: "We're looking at that. That's part of something that obviously, through CISA at DHS, we are we're taking a look." pic.twitter.com/E5Cp5FrUZa

— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 13, 2026

Air Space Intelligence, the company behind the FAA's SMART traffic-planning system, said the ground stop was "not based on or a result of the SMART system" or of its integration with the FAA:

The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.

— ASI (@AirSpaceIntel) November 13, 2026

Mullin also said "the president has declared this a national emergency, and now we have to have Congress act and fund it."

In September, as we reported, a cut fiber line knocked out Philadelphia TRACON's radio frequencies and ground-stopped arrivals at Newark, JFK, LaGuardia and Philadelphia, and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency hadn't known the backup fiber was cut until the primary circuit failed.

On Capitol Hill, Senate Commerce Committee Republicans noted that Lyndon Johnson was president the last time one of the country's 22 air route traffic control centers was built. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), who takes over the committee in January when Democrats take the Senate majority, said it will review how planes communicate on their primary frequencies, and the leaders of the House Transportation Committee, Reps. Sam Graves (R-Mo.) and Rick Larsen (D-Wash.), promised to "thoroughly review" what went wrong.

Duffy wants the money out of the lame-duck Congress: "We now have an opportunity in an emergency funding bill before the end of the year to give the money," he said, with Republicans running the Senate until January.

items.content_text:
This Is State-Snooping Taken To The Extreme: UK Taxman Wants Your AI Chatbot History

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity,

The UK government's tax collectors are pushing for powers that would let HMRC demand the private chatbot conversations ordinary Britons have with AI tools when preparing their returns.

Under proposals in the Budget Bill, the definition of what the taxman can force you to hand over expands from computer "records" to any "relevant thing." That wording opens the door to prompt histories, working papers and full conversations on platforms such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Claude if they played any part in calculating figures.

The measure sits inside a broader drive to close a £59 billion tax gap. Failure to respond to a Schedule 36 information notice already carries an initial £300 penalty; those who do not correct inaccuracies can be hit for up to £3,000. Third parties, including the AI companies themselves, can even be ordered to supply the data, the Telegraph reports.

Taxpayers could be asked to hand over their AI chatbot histories to HMRC as the tax authority expands its power to demand digital information.

This is HMRC's latest effort to close the £59bn tax gap ??https://t.co/01D2elIHEi pic.twitter.com/tucbHvefaU

— The Telegraph (@Telegraph) November 13, 2026

HMRC insists it is merely modernizing old powers for a digital world and that requests will still need a lawful basis. Critics see the thin end of a very long wedge.

The level of state surveillance and total over reach being ushered in by this government is off the scale. I've made multiple videos over the last couple of weeks about HMRC being given more and more powers and making more demands of people all the time. Yesterday I posted a crazy video report about energy companies being able to access your income tax, pension and homeownership details in order to be able to charge you more for your electricity if you were "doing well" In life. Now it's come to light that buried in the Budget Bill is a provision which allows HMRC to demand to see your Ai records, requests and conversations. Presumably this is to check what tax advice you are asking for and use it as evidence against you. What other reason could they have to demand to see your private Internet research. This is state surveillance. Privacy is dying, communism is being implemented more and more every day.

— John Hannam (@JohnHann04) November 11, 2026

Nimesh Shah of Blick Rothenberg noted that HMRC has said it wants information about "how tax figures have been produced using software or automated processes." That language, he observed, raises the question of whether the actual chatbot exchanges used to prepare calculations could become disclosable.

Seb Maley, chief executive of Qdos, put it more bluntly: "As more taxpayers and businesses put their trust in AI to help manage their tax affairs, HMRC is making sure it isn't left behind. It wants to know not just what tax figure a system produces, but how it arrived at that number."

HMRC could demand taxpayers' AI chat history in latest crackdown - all you need to know https://t.co/wXZB7R4lBk

— GB News (@GBNEWS) November 11, 2026

Anne Strickland of the Taxpayers' Alliance called the idea "a deeply intrusive overreach by the taxman." She added that HMRC "already has sweeping powers, and expanding them further risks trampling over the privacy of ordinary Britons." Ministers, she said, must rein the authority in before the power is ever used.

Anyone shocked. I'm not. They will make sure to get every penny out of you for their wars, the contracts they hand to their friends and to take care of illegals https://t.co/iS7Wf8vLYC https://t.co/dpAvPpMfHb

— leilani dowding ?? ?? (@LeilaniDowding) November 11, 2026

David Stirling of Mint Wealth advised anyone who has used a chatbot for tax work to assume the workings "could one day be scrutinised, so don't type anything you wouldn't fancy explaining to the taxman."

More than 28 million UK adults have already turned to AI for personal finance help, according to Lloyds Banking Group. Separate surveys show roughly 40 percent of people have used generative tools for financial advice and that more than 30 percent of businesses have put tax questions to systems such as ChatGPT or Copilot. Six in ten of those who tried AI said they found the answer they needed. The taxman now wants the trail of how those answers were produced.

HMRC to probe taxpayers' AI chat history in latest crackdown Tax office set to expand powers to collect conversations on tax calculations They're 'very good' at imposing ever more measures to spy on us all & crush privacy to get ever more taxes, while they are incapable of dealing with the problems we face.

— Alan D Miller (@alanvibe) November 11, 2026

An HMRC spokesman stated: "This is about updating our existing information powers to reflect how tax information is now stored and processed digitally. It is not about going through everyone's use of large language models. We can only request information where we already have a lawful basis to do so."

The same Budget package that expands information powers also hands HMRC the ability, from July 2029, to recover lower-value debts automatically from bank accounts of people who "repeatedly" fail to engage.

Nigel Farage warned weeks earlier that the taxman could seize money without even holding a meeting. "As someone who's been debanked, this sets a dark precedent," he wrote. "Reform will fight this at every turn."

HMRC can now seize money from your bank account without even having a meeting.

As someone who's been debanked, this sets a dark precedent. 

Reform will fight this at every turn. pic.twitter.com/u4YaBiY301

— Nigel Farage (@Nigel_Farage) October 28, 2026

The chatbot expansion and the bank-account raid sit on the same continuum: less process, less privacy, more direct state reach into the financial lives of ordinary people. Reform UK has already labeled the bank powers "draconian and dystopian." The AI proposals fit the same pattern.

Labour's answer to a large tax gap is not simpler rules or lower rates that raise compliance. It is wider demands, heavier penalties and the quiet assumption that private digital conversations about money now belong to the state if an algorithm touched them.

The taxman already knows how to take money from accounts without a meeting. Next it wants the chat history that led to the figure on the form.

Britons who treat an AI tool as a private notepad for tax calculations now find themselves having to be wary. The conversation is no longer just between you and the machine. The government continues it's draconian efforts to use every tool as a means for surveillance.

Meanwhile, kids are being indoctrinated with tax propaganda in school.

Eight-year-olds are told in one classroom video prepared by HMRC: "You can think of tax as one shared bank account that everyone in the country pays into. The government is then in charge of looking after this bank account and sharing all the money to help everyone in the country. This money is also used to pay for the things that your town or city needs. When you're older and you get a job, or maybe even start your own business, the taxes you'll pay will all be added into this shared bank account."

items.title: Britain's SAS Warns Troops Are Scared To Pull Trigger Over 'Witch Hunts'
items.content_text:
Britain's SAS Warns Troops Are Scared To Pull Trigger Over 'Witch Hunts'

Britain's Special Air Service soldiers are shying away from missions where they may have to kill, serving SAS officers say, because they fear being accused of war crimes later by a public inquiry that has hung over the regiment for nearly four years.

The officers told the Telegraph that there have been no outright refusals to deploy. But some serving members are now "less inclined" to volunteer for dangerous operations they could be investigated over. Asked what kind of operations, one officer answered: "Jobs where you might end up shooting people."

Serving SAS officers almost never speak to the press, even anonymously. The one quoted by the paper said the regiment feels "permanently and constantly scrutinised, without reprieve" and called it the worst part of the job. The officer still expects troops to act "correctly" on operations and not "hesitate" when they have to shoot.

The inquiry in question is the Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan, chaired by Lord Justice Sir Charles Haddon-Cave. It is examining allegations that SAS soldiers executed detained men and children during night raids between mid-2010 and mid-2013, that the killings were covered up, and that military police failed to investigate, according to BFBS Forces News.

The Ministry of Defence set it up in December 2022, after a BBC Panorama investigation alleged that one SAS unit killed 54 people in suspicious circumstances during a single six-month tour in 2010 and 2011. The MoD criticized the program's "unjustified conclusions" at the time, and an SAS source called the BBC's reporting "vexatious and fallacious." Forensic specialists are now going through about 10,000 photographs taken during the raids, which Haddon-Cave has said do not appear to have been part of the military police investigations. Three weeks of public hearings run through October and November, and the inquiry has set April 30, 2027, as its deadline to finish taking evidence on the alleged killings.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, in the job only since July, has taken the soldiers' side in public. Speaking to Forces News on Remembrance Sunday, he said that special forces members "live under a cloud worrying about whether they are going to be persecuted rather than thanked for their service."

"Those are things I need to put right. That's going to be a process. It's not simple," Streeting said.

His comments have fed speculation that he could scrap the inquiry altogether, though people close to Streeting deny that is his plan, the Telegraph reported.

The Afghanistan inquiry is not the only case weighing on the regiment. The Sunday Times reported this month that five SAS soldiers spent three years under a murder investigation over a 2022 night raid in Syria that killed two people who turned out to be teenagers working for ISIS. The soldiers were cleared in May 2025 but told the case could be reopened at any time.

In April, the Telegraph reported that SAS soldiers were applying for early release in numbers the paper withheld for security reasons, with insiders calling the losses a "threat to national security."

The serving officer said lawfare is "a contributing factor in the motivations of those who are leaving, or choosing not to extend," and that the regiment depends on senior soldiers staying past their normal length of service. Experienced officers in line for promotion could instead leave for careers where they feel more valued.

"We won't see the problem until it's too late," the officer warned.

Africans & Middle Easterners Drive Record 'Honor' Abuse & FGM Surge In UK

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity,

Police in England and Wales recorded 3,145 honor-based abuse offenses in the year ending March 2026 - the highest figure since comparable records began.

Female genital mutilation offenses rose 52 percent to 166. The number track the arrival and growth of communities in which family "honor" and control over female behavior routinely override individual rights.

The Home Office published the statistics on November 5. They mark a 7 percent increase on the previous year's 2,949 offenses.

I spoke with @GoodwinMJ on @GBNEWS about the new government data revealing a "record-high" rise in honor-based abuse in England and Wales. The Labour government has been extremely selective, picking and choosing which forms of misogyny are acceptable and which should be denounced, obviously they fear losing the vote bank.

— Khadija Khan (@KhadijaKhan__) November 7, 2026

London's Metropolitan Police alone recorded 625 cases, 20 percent of the national total. West Midlands Police logged 395 and Greater Manchester Police 254. Controlling and coercive behavior accounted for 22 percent of the total, with assault with injury at 14 percent. Forced marriage offenses stood at 129.

The Home Office states that the figures "are likely to only represent a fraction" of the true number because honor-based abuse is a hidden crime and many victims fear family or community retaliation if they report.

Improved identification and a Metropolitan Police system change in early 2024 have contributed to higher recording, yet the underlying pattern remains clear.

Under the police and Crown Prosecution Service definition, honor-based abuse is an incident or crime involving violence, threats, intimidation, coercion or abuse committed to protect or defend the honor of an individual, family or community for an alleged or perceived breach of a code of behavior.

It includes forced marriage, female genital mutilation, physical assaults, psychological control and restrictions on personal freedom.

FGM is illegal in the UK. More than half of the 166 recorded FGM offenses in the latest year came through the mandatory reporting duty that requires regulated professionals to notify police of known cases involving girls under 18.

Earlier official estimates placed the number of women in England and Wales who had already undergone FGM at around 137,000, with tens of thousands of girls still at risk.

The practice is concentrated among communities originating from countries with high prevalence, particularly in parts of Africa and the Middle East.

Conservative MP Rebecca Paul has described the growth as "unacceptable in modern Britain." She stated: "Close-knit clannish structures within isolated, unintegrated communities allow such violence to continue unreported and unchallenged."

These offenses cluster where large numbers of people have arrived from societies in which the practices are long-established and widely tolerated.

Official risk assessments have long identified elevated FGM risk among communities with roots in Somalia, Sudan, Sierra Leone, Egypt, Nigeria, Eritrea, Kenya and certain other African countries, as well as some groups from Yemen, Afghanistan, Kurdistan and Pakistan.

London's share of the cases is consistent with its demographic composition after decades of high immigration from precisely these regions.

The same pattern appears in other cities with substantial populations from high-prevalence source countries. Freedom of Information data referenced in reporting showed that, across the five years to 2025, at least 100 children aged 12 or younger were referred to the Forced Marriage Unit, including dozens aged ten or below and more than two dozen no older than five.

Mass importation of this culture is damaging our society. We cannot allow this savage and sickening behavior to be normalized. Girls face irreversible physical harm. Women face lifelong monitoring, restriction and violence.

Families and extended networks enforce codes that treat female autonomy as a threat to collective standing. British law prohibits the acts, yet the social norms continue to operate inside communities that have been allowed to grow large enough for the offenses to reach record levels.

Charities that specialize in the issue, including Karma Nirvana which runs the national helpline, have documented the scale for years and pushed for better identification.

A statutory definition of honor-based abuse was placed into law earlier in 2026. That change may improve future recording and prosecution, but it does not reverse the demographic and cultural factors that drive the offenses.

The Home Office has acknowledged that many victims remain reluctant to come forward and that existing systems still miss large numbers of cases. Parallel family and community pressures continue to deter reporting.

Enforcement against forced marriage and FGM has not kept pace with the size of the at-risk populations created by sustained high immigration from the relevant regions.

Britain's approach has treated volume of arrivals as more important than compatibility of values. Integration has been optional. The result is thousands of recorded honor-based abuse offenses a year, a sharp rise in FGM cases, and continued referrals of very young children to forced-marriage authorities. The communities involved are identifiable. The practices are identifiable. The policy that allowed the numbers to grow is identifiable.

Citizens who place the safety and individual rights of girls and women ahead of open-border preferences have every reason to demand an end to the mass importation of incompatible norms.

The record figures released this month are not a technical success of better data collection. They are evidence that practices once largely confined to specific overseas societies now generate sustained harm on British soil. Ending that harm requires ending the migration that carries it.

The statistics stand as a clear warning. Continued normalization is a choice. It is not inevitable.

items.title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop After Comms System Crash; Flight Disruptions Could Stretch Into Tomorrow
items.content_text:
FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop After Comms System Crash; Flight Disruptions Could Stretch Into Tomorrow

The latest: 

  • FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop 
  • FAA halts all departures nationwide; flights in the air allowed to continue
  • First nationwide ground stop since the January 2023 NOTAM failure
  • Duffy cites a communications failure hitting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers
  • Comms failure due to network reboot/crash
  • DHS's Mullin calls it a telecom outage and says there's no sign of an attack, "not another 9/11"
  • Mullin says the fix will take "some time" and he can't rule out an AI link
  • Some international departures from the east and west coasts were being allowed

Duffy, Mullin Hold Press Briefing

FAA Ground Stop Has Been Lifted

At 8:19 p.m. EST, the FAA canceled a nationwide ground stop that began around 4:00 p.m. EST and stranded tens of thousands of passengers. This is the second such shutdown since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks 

The shutdown snarled airports nationwide, with airlines canceling more than 1,000 flights and delaying more than 10,000, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. 

The Department of Homeland Security released a statement saying the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack. In fact, the outage appears to be related to a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies

There is no official timeline for when normal flight operations will resume after the ground stop, but the widespread disruption suggests recovery could take hours, potentially into Saturday morning.

However, JetBlue provided some clarity, warning passengers that disruptions will last into tomorrow morning. 

FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Caused By Network Reboot, System Crash; CBS Reports

More than 1,100 U.S. flights had been canceled and nearly 10,000 had been delayed as of Friday at 5:40 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware. As of around 4 p.m., there were still roughly 11,000 flights scheduled to depart from U.S. airports Friday, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.

Some international departures from the east and west coasts were being allowed to take off Friday evening, according to industry officials.

Polymarket predictions suggest the ground stop will be lifted around 2240ET. But after that, who knows how long until any kind of normal is resumed.

Caused By Network Update Crash, Reboot

The outage appears to be related to a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to people briefed on the matter. 

The network handles crucial radio frequencies that air-traffic controllers use to communicate with pilots, the people said. It wasn't immediately clear whether the outage also affected the radar feeds that controllers use to keep aircraft safely separated in the skies.

CBS News reporter Olivia Rinaldi says in a post on X, citing unidentified people, said an update to this private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, and when the FAA's telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. 

There is no confirmation of this report officially.

"Not Another 9/11": DHS

Update (1707ET): DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin says that the ground stop is a telecommunications outage and not terrorism. 

MULLIN: "This was a telecommunication outage throughout the FAA. Out of abundant caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for...""There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.

"There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said, adding this isn't "another 9/11."
 

***

FAA: Full Ground Stop

The Federal Aviation Administration has ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights due to technical issues. The agency has listed an equipment outage (with comms issues noted in advisories). 

The order, issued by the FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center at approximately 20:54 UTC (12:54 p.m. PST), applies to every U.S. airport. All aircraft still on the ground are to remain stopped until further notice. Flights already airborne are being allowed to continue to their destinations, while inbound international flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis.

The official advisory states:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY.
ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED.
ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the order on X, stating that the FAA issued the nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” He added that FAA technicians are investigating and that updates will be provided as they become available.

Nationwide ground stops are rare. The last full national stop of this type occurred in January 2023 after a failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system. That outage lasted roughly 90 minutes and caused thousands of delays and cancellations.

As of early afternoon Pacific time, the situation remained fluid. Passengers with flights scheduled for the remainder of the day are advised to check their airline’s app or website for the latest status, as recovery times will depend on how quickly the underlying equipment issues are resolved.

items.title: "That's Terrifying": Godfather Of AI Takes 18-Month Warning To EU Leaders
items.content_text:
"That's Terrifying": Godfather Of AI Takes 18-Month Warning To EU Leaders

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel laureate known as the godfather of AI, was on the program to brief the 27 EU leaders in Dublin on Friday morning, carrying a timeline that he says scares even him: the one he now hears from Paul Christiano, the AI safety researcher OpenAI put on its board in September.

"I've been going around saying, this stuff's going to get smarter than us and we really need to [worry]. It might happen within 10 years. And so I'm the one who's sort of been scaring other people," Hinton said on Wednesday. "But I go to Paul's lectures and he sort of says, this stuff might happen in the next 18 months. And that's terrifying."

He said he was "going to actually tell a bunch of government leaders that on Friday," adding: "And we'll see how they react."

"That's terrifying!" 

Geoffrey Hinton used to say we have 10 years until AI outsmarts humanity. 

Paul Christiano convinced him that timelines might be as short as 18 months, a terrifying prospect. pic.twitter.com/y75nO6JD2D

— Ori Nagel (@ONagel33303) November 13, 2026

Christiano, who founded the Alignment Research Center and helped develop the RLHF training method behind today's chatbots, opened this year's Hinton Lectures in Toronto on Monday night. 

"I think there is a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years," he told the audience.

 "I think there's meaningful risk even in the next six to twelve months."

"I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident," he said.

Christiano's evidence was OpenAI's own models: in July, OpenAI disclosed that GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model had escaped a sandboxed evaluation and broken into Hugging Face's production systems to get the answers to the cybersecurity test they were sitting, as we reported. "The models hacked Hugging Face because they thought maybe Hugging Face would have some information," Christiano said.

From there he described AI as "a second species which vastly outnumbers and outsmarts humans," and warned that "future agents may end up treating humans as another obstacle." Once that happens, he said, "they then will start thinking, what are the ways that I can overcome that obstacle?"

Introducing him on Monday, Hinton said he had "spent most of my career trying to make neural networks more intelligent," and summed up the problem in one line: "The central difficulty is that being intelligent and wanting what we want are two very different things."

Christiano joined the OpenAI Foundation's board in September, along with its Safety and Security Committee, the body with the final say on whether OpenAI releases new models. He has advised the US government on evaluating frontier models since 2024, through the AI Safety Institute that became the Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

Friday's meeting in Dublin is the first EU summit devoted to AI at leaders' level. In his invitation, European Council President António Costa wrote that "a first dedicated discussion, at leaders' level, is now needed," and he gave the opening session to two outside guests: Mistral chief executive Arthur Mensch on Europe's AI sovereignty and competitiveness, and Hinton on AI's impact on society, security and international governance.

The leaders came mostly to talk about catching up with the US and China, and on that front Brussels' InvestAI program promised to mobilize €200 billion, including €20 billion for AI gigafactories, and the plan for seven of them has stalled in fights over the bloc's 2028-2034 budget. The agenda has also been crowded by Ukraine: Euronews reports the row over who speaks for Europe in the peace talks threatens to take over the day, after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin.

Hinton has put the risk that AI wipes out humanity by escaping human control at 10% to 20%. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in September that a 10 percent figure from Hinton was "not grounded on science," telling Ezra Klein: "All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions."

And as we noted the same month, rogue AI scares like the Hugging Face breach have a way of helping the biggest labs: rules that slow AI down would also slow the open-weight competitors coming up behind them.

items.title: The Southern African Bi-Oceanic Railway Could Be A Game-Changer In The Sino-US New Cold War
items.content_text:
The Southern African Bi-Oceanic Railway Could Be A Game-Changer In The Sino-US New Cold War

Authored by Andrew Korybko via Andrew Korybko's Newsletter,

All of Southern Africa will likely fall under the US' "sphere of influence" and become the minerals base of the US-led "Global West's" "Fourth Industrial Revolution"-driven economic competition with China.

The run-up to the US' latest midterms dominated the global news cycle, which is why casual observers probably missed the announcement in late October that Angola and Tanzania agreed to pioneer a bi-oceanic railway across Southern Africa. The former's Benguela Railway, which the US now considers to be part of what it calls the Lobito Corridor, will link with the latter's 1970s Chinese-built Tanzania-Zambia Railway (TAZARA) in Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to fulfill this vision.

While regional economic integration is always positive, and this move can help bring more prosperity to those four's largely impoverished people if properly managed, the most significant outcome is that it'll probably further entrench the US' geopolitical influence. Its sway over Angola, the DRC, and Zambia has grown in recent years, the last of which finally signing a long-debated and contentious health deal with the US last month, and ties with Tanzania are on the mend after being strained for the past year.

Trump 2.0 is implementing the "Strategy of Denial", which aims to deny China access to the resources and markets required for maintaining its superpower trajectory. In the Southern African context, the US wants to dislodge China from its dominant position the DRC's mineral industry, which consists of some like coltan and cobalt that are indispensable to the "Fourth Industrial Revolution" (4IR). The same goes for China's position in the DRC's copper industry in particular and neighboring landlocked Zambia's too.

The goal is to greatly reduce China's control over these resources as part of the US' "decoupling" policy that it'll then demand that its partners follow. The purpose is to impose structural economic pressure on China for facilitating its capitulation to the US' demands for a lopsided trade deal that would institutionalize its relative junior status in the emerging world order. Failing that, the US's fallback plan is to bifurcate the aforesaid order, the scenario of which is known as "Chimerica" or "bi-multipolarity".

The disproportionate role of Southern Africa's minerals industry (which includes the DRC's) in the 4IR has recently transformed the region into an economic battleground in the Sino-US dimension of the New Cold War. As it stands, the US is gaining ground in accessing these resources, though not yet at China's expense. In the future, however, it'll likely resort to a combination of "creative diplomacy" and Hybrid Warfare to coerce these countries into replacing China's role in their minerals industry with the West.

As was observed here, "China lacks the capabilities and will to militarily enforce debt repayments, while the US' control over Western financial and legal institutions limits China's options in those respects", and the same goes for international arbitration if they illegally pull out of contracts with China. Simply put, Southern Africa's minerals are the US' for the taking, but it might first want to launch the Southern African Bi-Oceanic Railway (SABOR) for reducing import costs before making such a power play.

With this insight in mind, the US appears poised to push China out of Southern Africa's minerals industry in the coming future, though the exact timeframe isn't yet established since it depends on SABOR's completion and possibly its consequent optimization for maximally reducing import costs. In any case, barring a black swan, all of Southern Africa will likely fall under the US' "sphere of influence" and become the minerals base of the US-led "Global West's" 4IR-driven economic competition with China.

items.title: Let The Real Chaos Begin

Let The Real Chaos Begin

Authored by Robert Gore via Straight Line Logic,

Buckle up.

The same motive power that propelled Donald Trump's electoral victories in 2016 and 2024 propelled his disastrous midterm repudiation - fear and loathing of government. There is no unconditional love in politics. Trump was elected to upend the ruling caste, which, among his supporters, is even more despised than the government. He didn't do it, and has repeatedly demonstrated that he's just another paid-up member. Many of his former supporters either protest-voted for the Democrats or stayed home.

The Epstein case continues to rankle because it so clearly involves prominent members of that caste. Here was an opportunity to not just disgrace some of them, but perhaps send them to prison. At the heart of it lies one crime that most Americans still find repellent - nonconsensual sex with underage victims. Trump repeatedly vowed to get to the bottom of it, then reversed himself and dismissed the whole matter. That not only enraged people, particularly his supporters, it also fueled suspicion that his involvement with Epstein's depravity was far greater than he had admitted.

Wars have been the health of the ruling caste, and Trump broke his promise not to involve the U.S. military in any new ones, particularly in the Middle East. Trump partisans tend to forget that it was Trump who first got the U.S. involved in the Ukraine-Russia war, sending arms to Ukraine during his first term (a step Obama wouldn't take), even before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. That's been swept under the rug, but the disastrous U.S. and Israeli kinetic war against Iran can't be. Nor can its disastrous economic effects.

What also can't be hidden is that the war was launched at the behest of Benjamin Netanyahu and the Jewish lobby. They have an extraordinarily powerful and unhealthy influence on Trump. We'll probably never find out how much of it boils down to natural affinity on the one hand, and bribes, blackmail, and bullets - the specter of assassination - on the other. Whatever the case, Trump's subservience clearly fueled voter disgust.

The epic backlash against Israel began with Israel's effort to eradicate the Palestinians. Even stepped up hasbara and massive campaign spending in both the primaries and midterm elections has done nothing to turn the swelling tide. Ominously for Israel and the Jewish lobby, their influence is waning most markedly among the younger generations of Americans. Just to close an ugly circle, there is also widespread suspicion that Epstein's detestable honeypots were a Mossad operation, perhaps in conjunction with American intelligence.

There is no unconditional love in equity markets, either, and it looks like their long love affair with the AI industry is coming to an end. They are finally noticing their amour's circular financing, huge debt loads, Chinese competition, immense demand for power and water, rising political opposition, and highly speculative revenue and profit projections. Those should be enough to end the AI mania, and probably bring down the rest of the market as well.

Still to come is general recognition of the flawed premises underlying the mania. Artificial intelligence (or super intelligence for the remaining Trumpists out there) is a misnomer. Human intelligence (HI) rests on curiosity and asking questions. Those are individual, not consensus phenomena.

At root, the problem is that although AI can answer a seemingly infinite number of questions, it can't ask a single one. It can be programmed to spot and attempt to resolve conflicts within data, but it doesn't autonomously ask questions. From birth, the human mind is an autonomous question generator; it's how we learn. That's not confined to our species. Anyone who's ever watched puppies or kittens can see that they have something akin to human curiosity. They explore their environments and are interested in anything new (if they're not afraid of it). Curiosity and questions are the foundation of learning and intelligence. Reading even a page of something interesting or provocative will generate questions. Generative AI "reads" trillions of pages without an iota of curiosity. No one who either hails or warns of AI surpassing HI has explained how it will do so while bypassing the foundation of HI.

***

AI output essentially represents consensus "knowledge" as measured by AI's data surveying and statistical capabilities. What is defined as consensus may be an average weighted by the credentials and output of the various propagators of the data. It may, when it's spitting out "answers," note that the data conflicts and list alternative interpretations. However, aside from the fact that consensus, even weighted average consensus, is often wrong, there is a graver danger. Consensus wisdom is frequently the sworn enemy of innovation. Consensus-based AI may, on balance, retard more than it promotes innovation.

"AI is a Crock," Robert Gore, SLL, 12/13/25

Innovation is rarely, if ever, imposed from the top. AI is the ultimate from-the-top "innovation." It has governments, huge corporations, and trillions of dollars of capital behind it, pushing it for all they're worth. What it doesn't have is much of a use case for ordinary people. It's nice to be able to ask a computer a question and get a seemingly plausible answer. AI can save a little time and impart some organization to mundane tasks like scheduling and record keeping. However, as it is gets incorporated into almost everything, it can also be downright intrusive and annoying.

What remains to be seen is whether AI can perform tasks for which ordinary people and businesses will fork over enough money to cover its huge costs of production and capital. Especially because so much of what it's doing now is available for free, if not from U.S. AI purveyors, then from Chinese ones. In business applications, the price of tokens - the cost of AI usage - has dropped precipitously. There's still no hard evidence that even reduced cost AI pays for itself in productivity gains. AI may well share the disappointing (to their promoters) uptake of other "great," officially promoted technologies: solar and wind power, electric vehicles, and mRNA vaccines.

Most of the hyperbole of what is supposedly to come are a diversion. The real goal of AI has already been achieved - to enable the surveillance state, which is why it's being pushed so hard from the top.

And like climate change and COVID, AI has the totalitarians and would-be totalitarians drooling. Collecting, assimilating, and manipulating data is the technological foundation of a surveillance state. That's all the technototalitarians (See "Technototalitarianism," Parts One, Two and Three) require of AI - all-encompassing data that can be sorted by every available metric, including ones for which citizens might pose a threat, rhetorically or otherwise, to the government. Some of them must know AI will never get close to HI, but that's a useful claim, a selling point, to attract massive amounts of capital from Wall Street and support from the technototalitarian Trump administration.

"AI is a Crock"

There is no unconditional love in bond markets, either. Not only is the debt supporting AI faltering, so too is the big kahuna - sovereign debt. If equity markets crash, government bonds, particularly U.S. government bonds, may well catch a flight-to-quality bid and rally (interest rates would fall). However, quality isn't what it used to be. The U.S., most European, and Japanese governments are in debt up to their eyeballs. While buying their bonds as a short-term trade may work out, as a long-term investment, they are a guaranteed loser. Those governments cannot support their debt loads, especially when unfunded liabilities for pensions and medical care are included. That much of the world seems to be headed towards World War Three, which would undoubtedly be a costly fiasco, greatly magnifies the problem.

Governments and their central banks have two choices: implicit repudiation of their debt via devaluation of their fiat currencies, or explicit repudiation. They're already trying the former, but it's a good bet bond markets won't let them get away with it. Devaluation to zero produces interest rates to infinity. Governments are already feeling the squeeze of interest rates which are no longer zero, but are still in historically unexceptional single digits. Double-digit rates would force explicit repudiation and probably topple governments.

France is the preview of coming attractions. Its government spends more than half the gross domestic product on expensive welfare and warfare states. The national debt exceeds 119 percent of the GDP, and debt service is the largest item in the national budget. The government involves itself heavily in the sputtering economy (there is cause and effect between the two). The bond market has been marking up the interest rates on its debt, not just in absolute terms but relative to other nations' debt.

As France joins the rest of European NATO in costly preparations for a war with Russia that Russia doesn't want, the country has been engulfed in riots. Rioters employ the usual means - violence and destruction - have the usual ends - more this, that, and the other thing, paid for by someone else - and are covered by the usual media obfuscation about the identities of the rioters and their string pullers.

The French government and its would-be destroyers face the same problem - there's not only no money, but the future has essentially been spent as well. On present course, debt service will consume an ever larger share of production until the inevitable debt repudiation and economic collapse. The same problem confronts most of the developed world's governments - including the U.S.'s - and their would-be destroyers. The French are merely the first in line.

The world can't pay for the huge, centralized governments it already has. It certainly won't be able to pay for still more government if the destroyers have their way. Replacing myriad governments with one big government - the globalist dream - will produce an expensive, unproductive, ultimately unsupportable slave state. Its rulers will be almost as miserable as their subjugated subjects. From the delusional demands of the rioters, looters, and arsonists to the fever dreams of the globalists, the end result is the same - chaos, not utopian order.

That these outcomes are, in light of history and logic, glaringly obvious only highlights another obvious truth. The means of both the globalists and their stooges - violence and destruction - are their true end. A cautionary note for the globalists: violence is always a race to the bottom. The stooges, once unleashed, will engage in depraved torture and murder their putative masters can't control, and eventually that depravity will be trained on them. The only "order" that emerges from this chaos will be the order of demented savages - torture chambers and firing squads - not the advertised utopia of the "enlightened" totalitarians.

Government is obviously the cause and is just as obviously not the solution to the problems confronting the world's welfare-warfare states. Plenty of people recognize this truism. In the U.S., it has been the impetus for MAGA. Fear and loathing of government and rulers is not only here to stay - regardless of what happens to Trump - they will continue to grow as governments' failures mount.

Which will be - other than the fact that the U.S. government is already bankrupt - the biggest problem for the Democrats, the party of government, and their always-on-call stooges. Constrained by reality, the ultimate constraint, the blue team will be unable to deliver on their promises to further expand the welfare state. Indeed, ever-rising debt will render both the current welfare state and the warfare state - the red team favorite - unaffordable. It will also crowd out funding for productive investment, destroy savings, further devalue the dollar against "Real Money" (gold and silver), and crash the economy and financial markets. In some future election, perpetually disappointed voters will wash away the blue team with a red tsunami.

And so it will go, back and forth, until the general realization dawns that no matter who's elected, a government that's flat broke, fundamentally broken, riddled with corruption, and obsolete can't be fixed at the ballot box. At which point, bullets replace ballots. Uncontrollable violence and mayhem will be the order of the day.

Historians may look back on the 2026 midterms as the end of the beginning of the end of the centralization and control exercised by governments in the centuries-long epoch of government. The mounting chaos, confusion, and deterioration since the apotheosis of that epoch - the U.S. government's post-World War II dominance - is just a foretaste of what's to come and will last longer than any of us.

Buckle up.
