items.title: "It All Comes From The Israelis": Joe Kent Reveals What Happened When He Told Trump About Iran Intel
items.content_text:
"It All Comes From The Israelis": Joe Kent Reveals What Happened When He Told Trump About Iran Intel

Former National Counterterrorism Center director Joe Kent says Stephen Miller, now President Trump's chief of staff, "knew going into the Iran war that this was bad" - and that Miller's predecessor, Susie Wiles, gave pro-Israel voices time in front of the president over the intelligence community, while anyone who brought him bad news was asked not to come back.

Kent says it happened to him when he told Trump in the Oval Office that the Iran intelligence being briefed "all comes from the Israelis": CIA Director John Ratcliffe pushed back but "couldn't present anything" - and on his way out, Kent was told he wouldn't be needed at the next briefing. That was "a couple months" before "we let the Israelis drag us in."

Kent, who resigned in March over the war, told the story on the Shawn Ryan Show (episode #356, posted Nov. 12), his third time on the show. When he quit, he told Tucker Carlson that key officials were kept from briefing Trump, without saying who kept them out. This time he points at Wiles, whom Trump replaced with Miller on Nov. 6.

"It All Comes From The Israelis"

Kent says he and Tulsi Gabbard worried that intelligence reaching Trump wasn't being labeled with where it came from. On Iran, he said, it was "never being explained to the president that that information, lock, stock, and barrel, all came from Israel." "Not only did it just come from Israel, we really don't have a lot of unilateral, like our own intelligence collection, that can confirm or deny it," he added. Then he described the meeting:

"I had a personal experience where there was information being briefed to the president that was coming directly from the Israelis about Iran. And I interjected and I said, hey, sir, just for your awareness, all of that information on this topic about the Iranians, it all comes from the Israelis. And we don't have a lot of ways to independently verify it."

Ratcliffe disagreed and was "adamant" that other information confirmed it, Kent said. "He couldn't present anything. And he also couldn't prove that the intelligence report in question was not all from Israel. It was indeed all from Israel. So the president at least got that context there."

Kent said he was "promptly told as I left the Oval Office that day" that his services weren't wanted. "They just said, hey, we're not going to need you at the next briefing. We'll let you know if we need any, you know, counterterrorism advice or whatever," he said, allowing that it was "the president and his staff's prerogative."

As for who made the call: "I think Susie, for whatever reason, either she didn't want me telling the president that or she didn't want the friction between me and Ratcliffe."

"Not Allowed"

Wiles, a career lobbyist who came from Ballard Partners (the firm has denied pay-for-play accusations against her), decided who got to Trump on national security, Kent said. "She definitely prioritized letting in a lot of the pro-Israel voices to get time in front of President Trump, as opposed to having members of the actual intelligence community come in to give him United States intelligence," he said. "So Susie was definitely a gatekeeper. I mean, the president enabled that."

He said she once worked on Benjamin Netanyahu's re-election campaign in Israel and brought donors with her, Miriam Adelson among them, "very close" with Wiles. He also claimed AIPAC's leader is "on tape" saying AIPAC picked Ratcliffe, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and former national security adviser Mike Waltz. "She definitely enabled those people to basically serve as conduits to get Israeli intelligence to the president that helped get us into this war," Kent said.

Under Wiles, Kent said, "bringing the president any bad news or having any friction in front of the president was not allowed." "And if you brought things that were going to cause friction to the president or any kind of like bad news, you were asked not to participate anymore," he said.

Asked why Trump let her go, Kent said a strategy of "prioritizing the needs of the lobbyists in order to get the money to win the midterms" had failed, and Trump "needed to kind of blame somebody for the midterms" - while keeping the people who sold the war: Ratcliffe, Rubio and, "to a lesser degree," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. "This was such a massive intelligence failure. His entire intelligence team should be gutted," he said.

Miller Knew

On Miller, who has sworn "absolute loyalty" to Trump since taking over, Kent started with the upside: a longtime Trump speechwriter with a feel for the base. "I think he understands that like the Iran war wasn't popular," he said.

Kent said he dealt with Miller only "enough" to know where he stood. "I know that he knew going into the Iran war that this was bad. Like this was not a good thing."

The risk, Kent said, is that Miller "is like a hardcore Trump loyalist" who could settle for keeping the boss happy. If Miller tells Trump he is "going to be the polar opposite of Susie Wiles," brings in people "that have two different opinions" and tells him "how unpopular this war is," things could change. "But if Miller falls prey to, I just want to make the president happy and I want the president to always say nice things about me, which is the culture in the White House, then it's going to be no change from what we have with Susie Wiles."

Section 219

In the defense bill the lame-duck Congress is still working on, Kent said, "there's Section 219 that basically gives the Israelis unfettered access to some of our most sensitive programs, everything with quantum AI, ballistic missiles, everything that's sensitive. It makes them a co-equal."

Section 219 of the House's fiscal 2027 defense bill would set up a US-Israel defense technology cooperation initiative run by a Pentagon "executive agent." It survived in the $1.15 trillion bill the House passed narrowly in July, after Rep. Thomas Massie's bid to strip it was kept off the floor. Kent also pointed to a provision in the Senate's intelligence authorization bill that he says would give Mossad "unfettered access" to the intelligence community, the CIA in particular; that bill would expand intelligence sharing with Israel.

Israel may lose the nearly $4 billion a year it gets from Washington, Kent said, but a seat in the Pentagon's research programs is "going to be worth way more than four billion." He says Congress will try to pass both bills before January, and that Vice President JD Vance, as president of the Senate, should tell Republicans to "strip that out of there right now" or have it "used against us all in 2028."

Kent also has a book, part memoir and part account of "what went wrong" in the administration, now with the Department of Defense for redaction review.

items.title: Islamist Pilots Pose 'Insider Threat', Warn Security Experts
items.content_text:
Islamist Pilots Pose 'Insider Threat', Warn Security Experts

Authored by Paul Sperry via RealClearInvestigations,

When the Federal Aviation Administration reinforced cockpit doors after the 9/11 hijackings, it turned flight decks into fortresses to lock out terrorists. But what if a terrorist is already inside?

That question has new urgency following the harrowing Sept. 30 attack aboard a FlyDubai flight in which a Muslim extremist (Islamist) pilot was forcefully stopped by a heroic pilot and brave passengers from crashing a plane bound for Israel.

Former aviation security officials say the FAA needs to reassess threats inside cockpits and the measures intended to counter them. They say this review is especially urgent because the agency has made insider threats to the cockpit more likely by recently forcing airlines to add a secondary barrier to the cockpit in the form of a metal gate on new planes.

Experts say the added security, while well-intentioned, could backfire following al-Qaeda's call last month for Islamist pilots to carry out more suicide attacks inside cockpits and for followers to infiltrate the ranks of pilots. Al-Qaeda has reestablished terror training camps in Afghanistan, along with recruiting and propaganda organs, echoing its pre-9/11 potency.

Enhanced security measures designed to lock out threats could merely lock in an attacker. At the same time, the FAA is adding more people to the flight deck under a new training program that lets air traffic controllers sit as passengers in cockpit jump seats to observe operations up close, potentially opening up more security issues with relative "strangers" in the cockpit. All major U.S. carriers have agreed to participate in the program, which will vet controllers at the airport prior to takeoff but won't screen them in advance for extremist views.

Aviation security experts also say airlines must do more to identify pilots who may hold extremist views or show signs of mental illness. At least two U.S.-based Islamist pilots have been suspended in the wake of the FlyDubai incident.

"Pilots who have openly espoused and supported terrorists should be grounded as unstable," said former airline executive Michael Boyd, president of Boyd Group International, an aviation consulting firm, in an interview with RealClearInvestigations. "Anybody who supports clear terrorism should be grounded; but of course, that gets muddy in the realm of free speech."

Weak vetting systems

Suicide by aircraft has long been a rare but concerning issue. Most documented cases have involved private planes, not commercial carriers. Mentally ill people - including the German copilot who killed himself and 149 others on board when he locked the captain, who had gone to the bathroom, out of the cockpit and crashed a flight into the Alps in 2015 - have long accounted for most cases. But experts say a disproportionate number of such tragedies involving major airliners have involved Muslim pilots, most of whom have expressed extremist views.

During the FlyDubai attack, passengers were able to enter the cockpit and stop Omani copilot Hamam al-Hammami, an al-Qaeda supporter, who had attacked the flight's captain with an ax, from taking over the controls, thus saving the lives of the 174 mostly Israeli passengers on board. Gaining access to the cockpit - which the captain managed to unlock before collapsing - was the only reason the terrorist didn't succeed in crashing the jet into the Tel Aviv airport as intended after he disabled the captain.

While non-Muslims historically have been responsible for some cases of suicide pilots intentionally downing major airliners, three of the four cases directly linked to terror have involved Islamist pilots (9/11 is not included because it was a hijacking). Experts caution that the number is almost certainly higher because comprehensive data on the phenomenon is thin. Although most of the pilot-orchestrated terror attacks have taken place overseas, there is growing concern that American pilots aligned with terrorist groups like Hamas could crash airliners into U.S. cities.

Yet the FAA and Homeland Security currently have no system for vetting such sympathizers as insider threats, and are leaving it up to airlines to police pilots. Even Israel's Transport Ministry relied on Arab countries and their airlines to vet al-Hammami, whose long record of extremist views was overlooked.

Since the FlyDubai attack, United Airlines has grounded a Newark, N.J.-based pilot, Ibrahim Mossallam, after his social media posts praising the Oct. 7 Hamas attack were flagged. Israel recently barred another United Airlines pilot, Sina Amjadian, after he reportedly expressed support for Hezbollah and pledged loyalty to Iran's Revolutionary Guard in his own social media posts. Amjadian, who is of Iranian descent, is based out of LAX and previously flew for FlyDubai.

Mossallam was a former official for the controversial Council on American-Islamic Relations, acting as CAIR-NY's board chairman. He also served as a board member with American Muslims for Palestine, which is under federal investigation in connection with Hamas. CAIR did not respond to requests for comment.

Retired FAA special agent Brian Sullivan, who warned that Boston's Logan International Airport was vulnerable to a terror attack months before 9/11, told RCI that relatively lax screening of pilots is a "major hole" in U.S. aviation security.

"Vetting obviously needs to be given a hard look if we are going to keep bad guys out of the cockpit," Sullivan said.

The FAA and Homeland Security did not respond to RCI requests for comment. After the FlyDubai incident, the agencies issued official statements saying pilots must pass mental health evaluations, criminal background checks and security threat assessments, including cross-checking terrorist watchlists. Same for air traffic controllers, who will soon be joining pilots in the cockpit as jump-seat passengers as part of the FAA's new flight deck training program.

However, the agencies do not monitor pilots' or controllers' social media for extremist posts or photos to help predict if a cleared pilot will go "rogue" and weaponize commercial aircraft to carry out a religiously or ideologically motivated attack.

Jihadi pilots

While the majority of Muslim pilots are not extremists, Sullivan said dismissing the threat over concerns about "Islamophobia" or ethnic profiling ignores the reality of al-Qaeda's fatwa and the troubling history of jihadi pilots. He noted the FlyDubai incident is just one of several in which radical Muslim pilots have crashed or attempted to crash the planes they were flying.

In 1999, first officer Gameel al-Batouti seized control of EgyptAir Flight 990 while the captain was in the lavatory and crashed the plane into the waters off Nantucket while shouting, "Tawkalt ala Allah" (I rely on Allah) 11 times. More than 120 American and Canadian passengers perished.

In 2014, Malaysia Airlines Capt. Zaharie Ahmad Shah, a devout Muslim, was suspected of crashing his Boeing 777 into the Indian Ocean after plotting a course to the crash site on a flight simulator investigators found at his home. The alleged "rogue pilot" had also cut off radio contact and radar transponder transmissions before the jet and the 239 people aboard, most of them Chinese, perished. His motivation remains unclear.

In the Sept. 30 FlyDubai terrorist attack, al-Hammami ambushed and attacked the flight captain with an emergency axe after excusing himself to pray Islamic prayers. Two other Muslim pilots have reportedly been detained in connection with the plot.

"The latest incident raises serious questions about the risk entailed by both Muslim pilots and Muslim airlines operating in the United States," said Daniel Greenfield, a counterterrorism expert and fellow at the David Horowitz Freedom Center.

He said the number of suicidal Islamic pilots is likely larger than reported.

"It's unknown how many of the deliberate Muslim airline crashes were due to pilot terrorism because the Muslim countries involved tended to avoid any discussion of the motives involved," Greenfield said. "Some of the crashes by Muslim pilots have been attributed to personal issues, ranging from workplace frustration to a failed love affair; while others, notably EgyptAir Flight 990, were falsely attributed to mechanical failure."

That said, Muslims aren't the only pilots who have flown suicide missions. In addition to the Germanwings pilot, for example, a Japan Airlines pilot in 1982 pushed the engine controls in reverse during approach to Tokyo and crashed into Tokyo Bay, killing 24 passengers after suffering a mental breakdown. Some observers have called for broader psychological testing of all pilots rather than narrowly focusing on extremist Muslims.

Cockpit insecurity

Others worry that the recent exodus of veteran pilots from the industry following COVID-related buyouts is contributing to cockpit insecurity. De facto diversity quotas have led to the recruitment of pilots who are potentially less qualified and experienced, but also less known, critics say.

"How well do we really know the people that have our lives in their hands?" said Capt. Chris Pohl, a senior Virgin Atlantic training captain. "We should ensure experienced operational captains remain at the heart of pilot selection."

He argues that mass pilot retirements over the past decade due to a federally mandated retirement age of 65 have eroded peer-to-peer vetting that historically kept unstable pilots out of the cockpit.

"When I entered commercial flying, getting anywhere near a major airline's cockpit generally required substantial experience. Several thousand hours were often expected and those hours created a track record," Pohl said. "Most importantly, you developed a reputation. If somebody demonstrated poor judgment, a dangerous attitude or behavior that concerned other pilots, people often knew. Your reputation told them who you were.

"Today, a pilot can go directly from flying school to the right seat of an airliner with hundreds of hours, not thousands, with no employment history, just a license and exam results," he added.

Finding red flags

Some aviation security experts suggest federal regulators enhance the vetting process by using artificial intelligence to monitor the postings of pilots on social media for extremist content. AI-driven social media vetting could flag terrorist sentiments that could indicate plans for a suicide mission.

FAA regulators are also having to grapple with the issue of the mandatory emergency axe stowed inside the cockpit after the FlyDubai terrorist used it as a weapon to attack and disable the captain. Some experts say its use should be reevaluated. They propose replacing it with less lethal tools, such as heavy-duty pry bars or cold-cutting saws that don't produce sparks or flames.

"What they'll come up with relative to the crash axe will be interesting since it will pit safety questions versus security questions," Sullivan said.

The purpose of the axe is to allow pilots to hack their way out of the cockpit windows after a crash.

"The cockpit axe is a necessary safety item," Boyd said. "And like the cockpit controls, a crackpot pilot could make nasty use of it.

"That comes with the territory where we cannot defend against them," he added. "There's no way we can assure cockpits are completely loon-proof."

Still, the harrowing FlyDubai episode appears to have heightened the awareness of potential security risks from pilots.

"Hopefully, this will serve as a wake-up call to those who fail to address known vulnerabilities," Sullivan said. "We all know that aviation is still a viable terror target, and with Iran and other ongoing threats, this is certainly not the time to become lax."

Reuters offered more color on the drills:

During the latest drills, a Chinese submarine also launched an intercontinental ballistic missile ​from the Yellow Sea into the Chinese mainland, the official said. "It is a silent exercise — and in effect, silent intimidation," they said. 

"This is like a robber hiding a gun in the pocket of a coat — with the muzzle pointed at the bank teller. It scares the teller into handing over the money, while avoiding setting off the alarm and bringing in a ​large police response."

Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo described the military drills as "area denial" exercises involving an aircraft carrier and other naval formations.

On Thursday, Xi called for peaceful "reunification" in a policy speech without mentioning the use of force. Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its territory, has not renounced military action to bring the island under its control.

Beijing could pursue this move without military force by first using coast guard inspections, shipping restrictions, and selective interdictions, presenting them as domestic law enforcement around the island. CSIS identifies this as a possible move intended to remain below the threshold of armed conflict.

Our late-August report on a record Chinese ship swarm around Taiwan only reinforced our view that accelerating US-China decoupling would push investors toward conflict-free critical material supply chains that could benefit if shipping lanes around Taiwan became snarled, whether because of shipping restrictions or, worse, a blockade.

Iraq, Turkey, Pakistan Defy US Pressure, Refuse To Seal Borders With Iran

Via The Cradle

US efforts to pressure Iran’s neighboring states to close their land borders have failed, stalling Washington’s campaign to cripple the Iranian economy, the New York Times (NYT) reported this week.

Several of Iran’s neighbors have warned that cutting off trade routes vital to businesses and communities on both sides of the frontier could provoke “civil insurrection,” according to the US official.

He added that the pressure has stirred growing anger toward Washington among its allies and partners in the region. 

Turkey has largely maintained its border policies, while Baghdad has rejected US calls to keep only two Iranian crossings open. It briefly sealed one or two as a concession, angering Iraqis. 

Pakistan has reportedly closed and reopened several crossings in recent weeks, citing security and administrative concerns.

Ellie Geranmayeh, an Iran expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Iran retains considerable economic leverage over its neighbors. 

Beyond the $3 billion in annual trade with Iran, Islamabad relies heavily on Iranian fuel shipments, especially liquefied petroleum gas, while Baghdad draws more than a third of the gas that powers its electricity network from the Islamic Republic. 

Tehran has been taking its own measures, urging neighboring countries not to yield to US demands.

Iran’s deputy foreign minister met the Russian ambassador to discuss "how to counter unilateral U.S. actions, and the so-called Iron Gate plan."

On November 5, Putin hosted Iran’s Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, at the Kremlin. They agreed to build pipelines carrying Russian gas to Iran, enabling Tehran to meet domestic demand and resell gas to neighboring states. 

Rezaei said Iran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or negotiate until Washington meets seven conditions, including ending hostilities across the region, lifting the naval blockade and sanctions, and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

items.title: From Dynamism To Diatribe: How Republicans Lost The Plot
items.content_text:
From Dynamism To Diatribe: How Republicans Lost The Plot

Authored by Lipton Matthews via American Greatness,

Give credit where it is due, because the record is better than coverage suggests. Dismantling DEI ended a regime of compulsory ideological conformity in federal agencies and made diversity initiatives unattractive in corporations. Furthermore, the retreat from disparate impact theory by the Trump administration was explosive. For decades, statistical imbalance was treated as presumptive proof of discrimination, which pushed employers, lenders, and schools to manage outcomes rather than judge individuals. In December 2025, the Justice Department amended its Title VI regulations to eliminate disparate impact liability. That corrected a doctrine that had drifted far beyond what civil rights statutes required.

Environmental policy tells a similar story. The EPA repealed its 2009 endangerment finding on February 12, 2026, removing the legal keystone of a sprawling regulatory edifice built on agency interpretation rather than on laws passed by Congress. Climate and economic policy should come through democratic lawmaking, and builders and investors will notice that the burden of proof has moved back toward regulators.

Then there are Trump Accounts, perhaps the most underrated idea of this term. Washington deposits $1,000 into an investment account for every child born between 2025 and 2028 once parents sign up. Whatever one thinks of the branding, the principle is sound. It gives every child, including those from families that have never owned a share of anything, a stake in the productive economy from birth. Conservatives have long talked about an ownership society, and this is one of the few serious attempts to build one.

Why, then, did a party with this record take such a beating? It persuaded itself that Donald Trump was a sufficient centerpiece and that devotion to one man could substitute for a governing vision. In 2016, his message was short and aspirational: Make America Great Again. It spoke to people who felt their country had stopped working for them. By 2024, it had matured into a practical program of restricting illegal immigration, dismantling the DEI edifice, and growing the economy, which voters could weigh against their own lives. MAGA in 2026 offered no such thing. It had no liberating message, and it shrank from a movement of dynamism into a stale rant.

Start with the kitchen table. Coverage of results tied voter anger to high prices, the war in Iran, and concerns about government corruption. A party that campaigns against the cost of living should have had a vivid, memorable answer to it. Instead, families struggling with rent, groceries, and insurance were offered culture-war content. The Associated Press called the House for Democrats early on Wednesday and reported Senate flips in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, and Ohio. Voters rarely reward a party that is angry about everything except their bills.

Candidates matter too, and Republicans fielded too many weak ones. In Ohio, a state Trump won by double digits in 2024, Vivek Ramaswamy ran a political ad profiling his opponent's estranged mother that Ohio's governor and other Republican leaders condemned as unseemly. Amy Acton, who emphasized healthcare and affordability, became the first Democrat to win that governorship in 20 years. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico was projected to beat Ken Paxton for a Senate seat, and he did. Stronger nominees might have held both.

Ramaswamy's case is instructive for a deeper reason. His signature critique of America is that its culture venerates mediocrity, prizing prom queens over math champions and jocks over valedictorians. Hence his admiration for grind culture among Asian and immigrant families. It is a flattering story for a certain kind of striver, and it misunderstands what has always made America formidable. Its genius was never a regimen of tutoring and test prep. It was entrepreneurship and commercialization. Americans can turn anything into a business. They turned a hamburger stand into a franchise empire, a parlor game into a sports-betting industry, and a few friends with a camera into a media company with a candy line. That restless, slightly irreverent commercial energy deserves celebration, not correction by imitating someone else's study habits.

Nor does grind guarantee success. A subsistence farmer in a poor country labors longer hours than any engineer in Silicon Valley and remains poor because effort multiplied by weak institutions is still weak. Poland should have taught Ramaswamy this lesson. Since communism collapsed, it has become one of Europe's fastest-growing economies, and it did so without importing East Asia's grind model. Market reforms, rule of law, openness to trade, and a flourishing small-business sector did that work. Incentives and institutions, not an ethic of suffering, explain which countries rise. There is bitter irony here too. Ramaswamy's own primary challenger, Casey Putsch, made openly race-based attacks against him and courted far-right groypers.

That brings us to contempt. It ran from an obsessive hostility toward Israel, which hardened into something resembling derangement, to berating Indian Americans, among the most educated citizens in America. Online magazine right-wingers went overboard on immigration, sliding from a defensible case for enforcement and calibrated numbers into suspicion of newcomers and their children.

Whether an ethnonationalist concept of America is legitimate is irrelevant. It does not matter if cogent arguments exist that a nation is an extended family or that it is racial rather than civic. Most Americans find these ideas unpalatable, and in a democracy, that settles matters. Republican establishment figures overestimated the power of podcast land and underestimated ordinary Americans' contempt for tribalism and bigotry. MAGA podcasters bashing minorities or questioning the nationality of non-whites born in the United States unsettled even right-wing voters.

J.D. Vance compounded the error by behaving like a podcaster bro. He appeared on shows to criticize Israel as though that would win votes, and it did not translate into any. Many Republicans now blame the Iran war, and it clearly mattered, but that explanation is too convenient. Thomas Massie was his party's most strident antiwar voice, and yet he humiliatingly lost his seat. Opposition to war was real, but Americans were angrier at lackluster party leadership than at any single policy. Republicans had become defined by what they hated rather than what they would do.

Immigration shows this pattern. Deportations are necessary, yet not even most Republicans wanted to see ICE sweeping up people with no record of antisocial behavior and treating them like drug lords. Raids became a liability. Republicans also failed to read the room. They believed in a vibe shift even as Democratic Socialists ascended, and because they were impervious to evidence, they kept putting faith in podcasters and talking heads, as though ordinary voters care about podcast rantings.

Lampooning DEI became a hallmark of online right-wingers, to the point where posts would surface in my feed claiming that black students with above-average grades received offers from elite schools only because of DEI. A good argument against racial preferences degenerated into a stale rant. Even many who flirt with racial politics have black friends or non-white spouses, which is part of why such pitches ring false. There were serious efforts to do better. Groups like the America First Policy Institute tried to intellectualize Trumpism, and Fred Fleitz could make a coherent case for the Iran war, but these voices were dwarfed by imbecilic commentary from a host of bad actors.

Consider what was lost. MAGA at its best was a movement of energy, of builders, deal-makers, and people impatient with managed decline. It promised to get things done, and its signature achievements were policies. What replaced that dynamism was a feed of grievances. Had Republicans offered a positive message and stayed focused on policy, instead of polluting Twitter with diatribes against every non-white group, they would probably have done better. Racial and cultural controversies need not be suppressed. Such discourse can simply be conducted without impertinence. Republicans thought they were being "based" by resurfacing antisemitic and racist tropes, and voters canceled that basedness with a resounding Democratic victory. They must own their losses because, unfortunately, scapegoating Israel will not rescue them from the fangs of embarrassment.

Car Bomb Severely Injures Exiled Pro-Kremlin Ukrainian Official In Moscow

A targeted assassination attempt via car bombing has once again rocked Moscow. This time, the "pro-Kremlin" target survived, in what authorities are calling an attempted murder case and act of terrorism.

A onetime spokesman to former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov is said to be serious condition Friday in a local hospital, after narrowly surviving an explosion beneath his SUV in the south of the city.

The man has been identified as 72-year old Sergei Zavorotny. After the blast, reportedly the result of a magnetic bomb placed beneath the vehicle, he was quickly given first aid by passersby on the side of the road.

After formally leaving politics, Zavorotny has long worked as a journalist and commentator. Local reports suggest he's in very bad shape after barely making it out of the blast.

He was Prime Minister Azarov's press aide in Kyiv until 2014. BBC notes, "But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile."

Zavorotny - seen as a close Azarov confidant - has been sought by Ukrainian security services ever since:

In 2019 a Ukrainian court sentenced Yanukovych to 13 years in prison in absentia for treason, and Kyiv later placed sanctions on him and Azarov.

Zavorotny called the sanctions against his former boss emblematic of "a kind of Ukrainian-style McCarthyism, where local authorities simply 'snap to attention' and carry out the orders of their overseas supervisors," in comments to Russia's RBC newspaper.

Only the day prior, a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg. The blasts suggest that Ukrainian intelligence is once again ramping up assassination and sabotage efforts inside Russia.

The circumstances of Thursday's St Peternsburb blast were similar:

A Russian colonel has been killed in a car explosion outside St Petersburg, according to reports. Investigators have opened a murder probe after an unnamed serviceman died in the blast in the city’s Pushkinsky District early on Thursday.

A bomb is believed to have been strapped to the underside of the vehicle, detonating on the Kolpino Highway around 7am local time, according to local media.

An unnamed source told Russian outlet Fontanka that a colonel had killed in the blast while driving. A family member travelling with them was injured by shrapnel, they added.

items.title: $19,100,000,000,000: Americans Are Drowning In The Largest Ocean Of Consumer Debt In The History Of The World
items.content_text:
$19,100,000,000,000: Americans Are Drowning In The Largest Ocean Of Consumer Debt In The History Of The World

Authored by Michael Snyder via The Economic Collapse Blog,

Total household debt in the United States just hit a brand new all-time record high. For a large portion of the U.S. population, debt is a suffocating financial reality that never goes away. Millions upon millions of Americans found themselves drowning in debt the instant that they left college, and a very large percentage of them will still be deep in debt when they die. The entire system is designed to get us into debt and keep us there. 

Because a college education has become so expensive, most Americans have to go into debt to get one. Once you get out of school, you rapidly discover that you are going to have to go into more debt to get a vehicle or buy a home. And don't even get me started on medical debt. Most Americans, and this is especially true for those under the age of 40, are carrying mountains of soul-crushing debt. This is one of the primary reasons why young adults seem to be so angry all the time.

Many Americans that purposely tried to stay out of debt by living a frugal lifestyle have now been forced to take on debt by the rising cost of living.

At this stage, approximately 63 percent of all U.S. adults are living paycheck to paycheck, and 44 percent of Americans struggle to pay for even the most basic necessities.

When you are living right on the edge, it is so easy to go into debt when an unexpected expense suddenly arises.

You tell yourself that you are going to pay it off right away, but then something else comes up next month.

Of course if you end up getting sick and have to go to the hospital, that can set you back financially for years.

I can understand why millions of young people say that they are sick and tired of playing the game.

This week, we learned that total household debt in the United States has reached an all-time record high of 19.1 trillion dollars...

Total household debt rose $334 billion in the third quarter, to $19.1 trillion, according to new data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Even if we added nothing to that total from now on, it would take us approximately 52,293 years to pay off 19.1 trillion dollars of household debt at a rate of 1 million dollars per day.

Of course we are never going to pay off all that debt, are we?

The system is designed to keep increasing the total amount of household debt so that financial institutions can get even wealthier.

Credit card debt is among the most insidious forms of debt.

Last quarter, the total amount of credit card debt in the U.S. rose to a new record high of 1.29 trillion dollars...

According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, released November 10, credit card balances increased by $22 billion during the third quarter, reaching $1.29 trillion.

That's a 1.7% increase from the previous quarter and approximately 4.2% more than a year earlier.

The increase comes as American households continue to struggle with the cumulative effects of inflation, elevated borrowing costs, and other pressures on family budgets.

This should deeply alarm all of us.

According to Consumer Affairs, credit card balances have "increased by approximately 61% over the past five years"...

Credit card balances have increased by approximately 61% over the past five years, according to an analysis of the Fed's data by American Banker. The total first crossed the $1 trillion threshold in 2023.

Sadly, we owe even more than that on our auto loans and our student loans...

Auto loan balances increased by $21 billion to $1.73 trillion, while student loan balances rose by $5 billion to $1.66 trillion.

Home equity lines of credit increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, the largest quarterly increase in that category since 2005.

The average length for a loan on a new vehicle is now 69 months.

The reason why payments are being stretched out for so long is because the average price of a new vehicle has hit $51,109...

The average price of a new vehicle in the US has climbed to a record $51,109, according to a new Cox Automotive report citing Kelley Blue Book data. Combined with new-car loan rates near their highest levels since the mid-2000s, record sticker prices are putting vehicle ownership increasingly out of reach for many working-class folks, even before insurance, fuel and maintenance costs are factored in.

The vast majority of Americans cannot afford to purchase a new vehicle.

In fact, used vehicles are now out of reach for much of the population.

Our standard of living is declining right in front of our eyes, and that should be obvious to everyone.

When I was growing up, homes were being rapidly constructed all over the country and they were quite affordable.

But now homes are insanely expensive and home sales just fell to their lowest level in 16 years as a result...

Home sales declined in October to their lowest level since 2010, a new trough for a housing market that has been hovering near rock bottom for more than four years.

Sales of existing homes fell 5.5% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday, marking the steepest decline since January. Economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal expected a decline of 3.8%.

This is not what prosperity looks like.

Decades of very foolish decisions have destroyed our standard of living, and the outlook for the future is exceedingly bleak.

U.S. households are 19 trillion dollars in debt, and the federal government is 40 trillion dollars in debt.

How can anyone possibly claim that this is going to end well?

Earlier today, I came across an article about the sinking of the SS United States...

The historic SS United States, once the fastest ship on the seas, made a slow final journey beneath the waters Wednesday.

The famous ocean liner - which is longer than the Titanic and crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times - was deliberately sunk Wednesday to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico, where the once-luxurious behemoth was set to begin a new chapter as the world's largest artificial reef.

It was a long goodbye.

Hours after the sinking began on a cloudy afternoon, much of the hulking ship could still be seen in the dark waters off the coast of the Florida Panhandle by nightfall.

Just like that ship, our economy was once a magnificent vessel.

But now it is also sinking.

Previous generations handed us the keys to the most robust economy in the history of the world and we wrecked it.

We obviously did not learn anything from our mistakes, because we just elected the worst group of lawmakers that I have ever seen.

It has been said that debt is the worst form of poverty.

In other words, owing money is worse than simply having nothing at all because you are starting below zero.

Our leaders were able to keep the party going for a long time, but now a moment of reckoning is at hand and the collapse that is starting to unfold is going to be incredibly painful.

items.title: "He Wants This To Go Fast": Nvidia's Top Lawyer Kept Name-Dropping Trump To Strong-Arm Regulators, According To Report
items.content_text:
"He Wants This To Go Fast": Nvidia's Top Lawyer Kept Name-Dropping Trump To Strong-Arm Regulators, According To Report

Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter told more than a dozen government officials working on terms & conditions for the company's H200 chip exports to China that he was in a meeting with President Trump and Jensen Huang to discuss the issue, Semafor reported Friday.

"He wants this to go fast," Teter said on the January call, according to people with access to a detailed account of it. The line went quiet.

In order to remain compliant, chip sellers would be required to know who their cloud customers were before shipping and to vet anyone buying more than a few thousand chips (recall China's 'technically legal' loophole). Teter called the cloud-customer requirement a deal-killer for Nvidia, and the company pushed to raise the vetting threshold to the tens of thousands of chips, billions of dollars' worth, and to limit end-of-life conditions to chips already under export controls.

According to the report, Teter bandied about DC name-dropping Trump to try and grease gears. In one exchange the outlet viewed, he accused officials drafting export restrictions of misrepresenting Nvidia's products and Trump's policies, and scolded them for not carrying out the president's agenda.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, meanwhile, said it is routine for agencies to work with individual companies on license conditions, which often change in response to legitimate business concerns, and that the State, Defense, Energy and Commerce departments sign off on the final versions.

The Megaspeed Calls

Five months before that call, Teter emailed the Commerce Department agents building a smuggling case against Megaspeed, telling them Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler had given Nvidia permission to reach out, as we reported. Megaspeed is the Singapore data center company whose former executive, Alice Huang, is the suspected Chinese spy Jensen Huang has acknowledged a relationship with.

The Justice Department took control of the probe shortly afterward, with some officials there worried that Kessler's contact with Nvidia "had tainted the investigation," the Wall Street Journal reported. DOJ now runs a criminal inquiry. Commerce says Kessler never ordered information shared with Nvidia and that the bureau handles enforcement by the book.

Nvidia gave the bureau an incomplete account of its business with Megaspeed in the months after Teter's late-summer 2025 call to Kessler, Bloomberg reported.

Nvidia told Bloomberg that Teter didn't know about Huang's affair when he contacted Kessler, and says its outreach to Commerce was meant to provide information and help stop illegal transshipment. The company says it cut off all sales and shipments to Megaspeed in June 2025. Malaysian trade records show Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 of Nvidia's GB300 processors, worth about $787 million, in November 2025, according to Bloomberg.

Huang, who resigned as CEO on Thursday, has said there was no evidence Nvidia's chips were being diverted to China. Bloomberg has since reported that the Megaspeed sales Nvidia disclosed to the US government came up about 50,000 chips short, worth billions of dollars.

The Tracking Nvidia Said It Couldn't Build

Nvidia told congressional staffers in 2025 that a Chip Security Act provision requiring chipmakers to be able to locate their chips couldn't be done, former staffers told Semafor. It would take entirely new technology, the company said, and even then the tracking would be easy to spoof.

Nvidia's lobbyists also warned committee staff that location tracking would open up cyber vulnerabilities. One former staffer said the committee spent six months going behind Nvidia to undo what it had told other offices. Others said the company counted on most Hill aides lacking the technical background to push back, and got a range of bills weakened that way.

In August 2025, Nvidia's chief security officer argued in a company blog post that building backdoors and kill switches into chips "would be a gift to hackers and hostile actors." Reuters reported the post as Nvidia urging Washington against location verification.

Four months later, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters that it had built location verification software, as we noted at the time. It had been demonstrating the feature privately for months, and launched it in May. One former staffer accused Nvidia of lying to Congress about whether tracking was feasible while it was building the feature into its next generation of chips.

Megaspeed Still Isn't Blacklisted

Officials were weighing whether to add Megaspeed to the Commerce Department's Entity List as early as spring 2025, a former State Department official told Semafor, earlier than previously reported. A former Commerce official said the department can blacklist a company extremely fast when it wants to.

As we noted on Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent allegedly confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in the White House Situation Room on Nov. 5 over why Megaspeed still isn't on the list; Commerce denied the exchange took place. On Friday, Bessent said Treasury, War, USTR and State "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months," and Lutnick agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

items.title: Operation TorNado: 354 Arrested, $234 Million Seized In Global Dark Web Drug Crackdown
items.content_text:
Operation TorNado: 354 Arrested, $234 Million Seized In Global Dark Web Drug Crackdown

Authored by Jacki Thrapp via The Epoch Times,

U.S. and international authorities arrested hundreds of people and seized drugs, guns, cash, and cryptocurrency in Operation TorNado, a crackdown on dark web sales of fentanyl and other drugs, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said on Nov. 12.

The department put the total at 354 arrests and said the cash and cryptocurrency seized were worth more than $234 million.

Vendors and buyers on dark web marketplaces such as Archetyp, Bohemia, Nemesis, Kingdom, and Tor2Door were caught in the crackdown.

The arrests included 132 in the United States, 59 in the UK, 45 in Hungary, 41 in Germany, 23 in France, 13 in New Zealand, 12 in the Netherlands, 11 in Slovenia, six in Austria, five in Ireland, four in Czechia, two in Australia, and one in Finland.

The department described Operation TorNado as a coordinated, multi‑agency, and international law enforcement effort.

The department's Joint Criminal Opioid and Darknet Enforcement (JCODE) team and Europol jointly announced the results, marking the latest operation in their ongoing partnership against illicit trade on the dark web.

"Operation TorNado represents the sixth - and most extensive - internationally coordinated action since JCODE was created in 2018," the DOJ said.

An undisclosed number of investigations are still underway to identify people behind dark web accounts.

The SpeedyPharma Case

One of the suspected drug traffickers was Jonatan Gonzales, 35, of South Bakersfield, California. Gonzales, known by the dark web distributor name SpeedyPharma, allegedly used his home to ship illegal drugs to multiple addresses across the country.

Law enforcement officers seized 48 pounds of methamphetamine, 386 grams of black tar heroin, 588 grams of cocaine, $40,565 in cash, 2.8 grams of carfentanil, and 3.5 grams of fentanyl at his home.

"Now that might not sound like a lot of fentanyl, but remember, the potentially lethal dose of fentanyl is just 2 milligrams," Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 12. "That means that the amount of fentanyl seized at his residence was potentially lethal to over 1,700 people."

Blanche elaborated, saying that the amount of fentanyl, if taken, could kill everyone in a small town or a graduating class of high school or college.

"There's no doubt that Operation TorNado saved lives across the country, and there is nothing that will stop this administration's commitment to protecting the American people from synthetic drugs, which are lethal," he said.

.@AGToddBlanche: "There is no doubt that Operation TorNado saved lives across the country, and there is nothing that will stop this administration's commitment to protecting the American people from synthetic drugs, which are lethal." https://t.co/P7fyEZx63t pic.twitter.com/SEndKxuXp4

— U.S. Department of Justice (@TheJusticeDept) November 12, 2026

Gary Barksdale, chief postal inspector of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, said the accused criminals were "exploiting" the service and other carriers in order to ship the drugs.

"When they utilize the mail for those transactions, these criminals threaten the safety of postal employees and the integrity of the postal network that hundreds of millions in the U.S. and across the globe depend on every day," Barksdale said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said his agency has accelerated cyber capabilities with a newly established Cyber Branch, which is evolving to meet threats on the dark web.

"The success of Operation TorNado makes clear that criminals cannot hide behind technology or geography - no matter where you operate, justice will find you," Patel said.

items.title: The Nuke Question: Wall Street's Top Defense Analyst Says US Nuclear Use In Iran "Cannot Be 100% Ruled Out"
items.content_text:
The Nuke Question: Wall Street's Top Defense Analyst Says US Nuclear Use In Iran "Cannot Be 100% Ruled Out"

For eight months, every Iran headline has come with the same two-way trade: peace deal on Monday, "locked and loaded" by Friday.

This week was no exception: Monday, November 9 was the date that a handful of media reports had penciled in for the resumption of major US strikes (a new moon, three carriers on station, the midterms safely in the rearview mirror). Instead, President Trump walked out of a meeting with Qatar's prime minister and told reporters that military action against Iran does not seem necessary at this point, one day after telling CNN that new bombing is "highly unlikely" if talks progress. Stocks responded with an everything rally, with the S&P closing up 2.4%, while Brent slid back below $95, extending what was already its biggest weekly drop since the Covid crash.

And yet, in the same 72 hours the US carried out what Trump called "minor" strikes on Qeshm Island (which have continued since), the IRGC reported three more tankers ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz (with more tankers catching fire through Friday), a Houthi missile damaged an Aramco tower in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was hit in the Medina region, and Secretary of State Rubio said no breakthrough was in sight. Peace, in other words, is going great.

Which brings us to the best single piece of sell-side work we have seen on where this war goes next. In a note published on election day and titled "Lots of Variables in Resumption of Middle East War. The Nuke Question" (available to pro subs), Capital Alpha's veteran defense analyst Byron Callan does something that very few of his peers have been willing to do: he admits he has no idea whether the US and Israel hit Iran at scale again in November or December, and then explains why the answer may matter less than what the next round would cost. As he puts it:

Maybe the U.S. and Israel strike Iran at scale again in Nov.-Dec. 2026, and maybe they don’t. Markets seem to have fainting spells every time there is hope of a peace deal, but there is precedent for negotiations being abruptly cut off as strikes commence.

In other words, the market keeps pricing the last headline, while the people with the bombers keep their options open. Regular readers will recall that negotiations were also "progressing" in late February, right up until the morning of February 28.

And then there is the part of the note that gave it its title. Callan very much doubts that Washington would ever use a nuclear weapon on Iran's deepest bunker, but in his words the possibility "cannot be 100% ruled out." When the dean of Washington defense research feels the need to put that sentence in writing, well, it is probably worth reading the rest.

Air Power Can Punish. Toppling Is Another Matter

Start with what the US and Israel can actually bring to bear. Callan's read is that the balance of forces has barely changed since the spring campaign:

  • Two US carriers with roughly 96 combat aircraft, plus submarines and destroyers that add cruise-missile capacity. (It may be three now: Trump told CNN on Sunday he has three carriers in the region, although Goldman's Rich Privorotsky notes the USS Theodore Roosevelt is not expected before mid-November. Pick your source.)
  • The Israeli Air Force has the same number of combat aircraft and tankers as in February and March, and has probably rebuilt some, but not all, of the strike weapons it burned through.
  • Bombers and tankers are available, but where they would be based is an open question, as is whether the Pentagon is willing to park F-15Es at bases in Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and maybe Israel that lack shelters against missiles and drones.

That last point is hardly academic: when Iran fired about 20 ballistic missiles at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on September 8, aircraft on the ground were damaged despite a salvo of more than 70 interceptors.

What about boots on the ground? Callan does the arithmetic for anyone still entertaining the idea: two Marine Expeditionary Units, each with a Battalion Landing Team of about 1,200, plus elements of the 82nd Airborne, are not marching on Iranian cities and installing a new government. Trump seems to agree.

So that leaves the air campaign, and here the Capital Alpha analyst is blunt:

We have also been extremely skeptical that a strategic air campaign alone would lead to regime change. A strategic air and missile campaign could make life miserable for Iranians, impose costs on the Islamic Republic and IRGC, and further reduce its economic capacity, but the bulk of the Iranian military and IRGC is likely to survive.

Put differently, a second Epic Fury can make Iran poorer and angrier, but the bulk of the Iranian military and the IRGC probably survives it. This is the same conclusion US intelligence reached two weeks into the war, and it is why Treasury Secretary Bessent pivoted in August to collapsing the regime through economic warfare instead. Trump's own pitch on Sunday was that the US has picked out 38 bridges it can drop in an hour, and that Iran is running 301% inflation.

Bridges are easier to knock down than regimes.

The Interceptor Math Still Doesn't Work

The second leg of Callan's argument is that Iran gets a vote. Tehran has promised a widespread response to any new campaign, and while the US and Israel have partly restocked their air-defense interceptors, he reads the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia as evidence that the shortages remain significant. Iran's own missile and drone inventories are smaller than they were in February. They are not zero.

Sunday's hole in the side of an Aramco office tower, in a kingdom that spent $83 billion on defense last year, makes his point better than any spreadsheet. So does the September 8 attack on the Jordan base, where US forces fired 60 to 70 Patriots (about $4 million each) and more than a dozen THAADs ($12 million to $15 million each) to defend a single target. On our napkin that is roughly half a billion dollars of interceptors for one night's work, against an industrial base the Pentagon's own inspector general says has run into "strategic inventory shortfalls."

From there the note turns into a list of five things Callan says he cannot assess, which doubles as the most honest summary of the war's second-order effects we have come across:

  • How many more U.S. air defense interceptors and strike weapons would be consumed?
  • Whether it’s possible to further increase production rate targets in 2029-32 for U.S. weapons?
  • How is Iran assessed as a military threat in 2027-32?
  • What will countries in the region do if they can’t get timely resupply of U.S. interceptors and possibly ground control units and radars? Where else do they turn to?
  • How does further depletion of U.S. weapons inventories shape risk-taking by China, North Korea, and Russia in 2027-32?

Translation: every interceptor fired over Riyadh or Azraq is one that is not sitting in Guam, Seoul or Poland, and Beijing, Pyongyang and Moscow can count. The Gulf states can count too, and if Washington cannot resupply them on time, the question of who they call next (Seoul? Ankara? Kyiv?) will shape defense order books for a decade.

Hormuz Is "Open" The Way A Minefield Is Open

On energy, Callan declines to forecast what a strike on civilian and energy infrastructure would do to the world in 2026-28, since it depends on what gets hit and by whom. He does offer two observations. First, any further jump in energy prices is more worrying now that global reserves have been drawn down. Second, he has never bought the idea that the Strait of Hormuz is open in any pre-February 28 sense: the UK's maritime trade office would hardly be logging near-daily reports of merchant ships struck by unidentified projectiles if the waters were safe.

He also cites a recent post by Radigan Carter putting VLCC day rates at $30,000 before the war and $600,000 now, or 20 times higher. Having tracked the tanker rate crisis since February 20, before it was cool, and all the way to the $1 million tanker, we would only add that the number moves by the day and the direction of travel depends entirely on who mined what that morning.

Today's news fits the pattern. The East-West pipeline, the kingdom's main Hormuz bypass, was hit again, and while the energy ministry says the fire was small and flows were unaffected, this is the same line the Saudis had to shut in September. We have been warning since March, when Fujairah was in flames, that the bypass routes would become targets in their own right.

So how is the Street handicapping the next move? JPMorgan's Market Intelligence desk (available to pro subs) relayed this morning how the bank's Center for Geopolitics frames Washington's menu:

  1. An Epic Fury 2.0 that revisits the kinds of military targets struck in the spring
  2. Broader attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure
  3. A “final blow” aimed at a nuclear target, a largely performative strike that would allow Washington to declare “mission accomplished.”
  • The team also noted that Washington has had these same options on the table since the MOU collapsed in June without reaching for them, given all risk Iranian retaliation and an escalatory spiral sending energy prices even higher and inflicting considerably more economic and psychological damage across the Gulf

The third item on that list, a largely symbolic strike on a nuclear site that lets Washington declare victory and go home, is the one to remember when we get to Pickaxe Mountain below. 

As for odds, JPMorgan's commodity traders went into the weekend with a coin flip: 50% that more strikes come (followed by a declaration that the military phase is over), and 50% that diplomacy gets more time. Within the strike branch, they put 75% on the US staying to police Hormuz and keep the blockade, and 25% on a full exit.

The diplomacy branch called for a $4 to $5 drop in Brent and a 7 to 10 point fall in volatility as January length gets dumped, which is the direction the tape took this morning, with WTI down almost 3% (helped along by hedge funds that had already puked $6.6 billion of Brent into the midterms). It is also a long way from the 90% odds of "Round 3" that were doing the rounds on October 20.

Goldman's Rich Privorotsky, for one, is not convinced that the calm survives the week. In his morning note (available to pro subs), the head of the bank's EMEA one-delta desk flagged the mixed messages from Trump and Rubio and then offered a calendar:

The USS Theodore Roosevelt is not expected in the region before mid-November. Absent tangible diplomatic progress, I’d expect escalation premium to return to oil by Wednesday/Thursday ahead of the weekend.

Which is the Monday de-escalation, Friday re-escalation pattern we have been pointing out for months, now with a Goldman stamp on it. It also squares with the bank's commodity team, which last week found that a roughly $27 risk premium explained most of October's crude rally, and with the physical market, which has since flipped from bidding war to fire sale.

The Nuke Question

Now for the part nobody on the Street wants to model.

The speculation has been building since mid-October, when the Pentagon was reported to be eyeing the "Mother Of All Bombs" for the next round and Trump, asked directly, said he would not go nuclear. It went into overdrive on election day when Tucker Carlson claimed, without evidence, that the administration was days away from a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain (the White House waved it off), and again last Friday when The Times reported that Iranian authorities were handing out iodine tablets near nuclear sites.

We covered the iodine story in detail on Friday, and have been writing about the site itself since July. Callan's contribution is to treat the question like an analyst instead of a pundit: he does not expect it, he will not say the odds are zero, and he walks through what the weapon would actually do.

The target first. Pickaxe Mountain (Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La) peaks at 1,593 meters, sits about 2 km from the Natanz complex and roughly 100 km north of Isfahan, a city of about 2 million people.

Then the weapon. The B61 is a gravity bomb that comes in several versions, one of which is an earth-penetrator that a B-2 can deliver. Its yield can be dialed down from a maximum of 400 kilotons. For context, the two bombs dropped on Japan in 1945 came in at 15 to 20 kilotons.

The penetrating version has a hardened nose that lets it dig several meters into soil and rock before it goes off, and most of the damage to anything buried underneath comes from the shockwave, which could collapse tunnels and halls.

And here is the catch. "Several meters" is nothing like an underground test. Callan presumes a risk that radioactive material gets out, and points to Brookings for the comparison: US underground tests in Nevada were buried between 600 and 5,000 feet below the surface. The halls under Pickaxe are reported to sit 80 to 100 meters down.

In other words, a bomb with up to 27 times the yield of Hiroshima would be going off about as deep as a basement, two kilometers from Natanz and upwind of somebody. Which is presumably why Tehran is handing out the iodine.

Radiation aside, Callan lists three more reasons the idea is a bad one, and for a defense analyst the second is the most interesting:

  • Using a nuclear weapon could remove a prohibition that has existed since 1945. It could raise the possibility that Russia uses nukes against Ukraine. It could also prompt other countries to seek their own nuclear weapons.
  • An administration decision to use a nuclear weapon could radically polarize U.S. domestic politics and relations with other allies. That’s probably not positive for the DoD/DoW budget or for U.S. defense exports.
  • Without independent verification, there would be no way to determine whether everything under Pickaxe had been destroyed and unsalvageable if a weapon was used.

Take them in turn. A taboo that has held since 1945 goes away, which Russia would notice in Ukraine and every would-be proliferator would notice everywhere (Trump himself said in September that he would not have bombed a nuclear-armed Iran, which is about the most effective advertisement for getting a bomb ever recorded, and Iran's hardliners have been listening). US politics and alliances would be polarized to a degree that is probably negative for the Pentagon's budget and for US arms exports. And with no inspectors on the ground, nobody could confirm that whatever was under the mountain was destroyed.

That last one is the killer. The entire point of the third option on JPMorgan's menu is to be able to say the job is done. A weapon that breaks the biggest taboo in warfare and still leaves you unable to prove it worked fails on its own terms, and that is before Iran told the IAEA today that it does not consider itself bound to full monitoring while under threat of US attack.

For The Defense Trade, November Matters Less Than 2027

So what does any of this mean for the stocks? Callan's answer is that the implications cut both ways, and his broad views are unchanged: whatever happens in November and December probably matters less than i) how Iran is perceived as a military threat in 2027-35, ii) whether the US is still seen as a reliable security partner, and iii) what Middle East governments decide to do about their own security.

That is a longer horizon than the market has been using. Defense names sank after the Democratic sweep, with Lockheed (LMT) and Northrop (NOC) down 3% and Goldman's European defense basket falling as much as 4.1%, as TD Cowen's Roman Schweizer called the result the toughest outcome for defense spending and warned of a flat to low-single-digit FY27-28 topline and a new War Powers fight. That came on top of a sector that had already fallen out of favor in September.

Goldman's trading desk thinks the selling has gone too far. Privorotsky calls the derating extraordinary and sees a path for Washington to hold the topline anyway:

More interesting is the extraordinary derating in defense. In the U.S., Washington could ultimately maintain top line defense spending as part of a lame duck compromise with Democrats on healthcare. Meanwhile, European defense looks increasingly asymmetric: ceasefire headlines and EU fiscal debates have driven multiple compression, yet structural NATO 2%+ GDP commitments and multi year order backlogs mean a lot of bad news is already priced in.

And the bank's industrials specialist Ryan Novak, in a note this morning titled "A&D from here" (available to pro subs), makes the fundamental case that maps most directly onto Callan's interceptor math:

We also come away positive defense primes as well though acknowledge the very recent outperformance in the bid to “defensives” creates a slightly higher bar than we wish. However, taking a step back, we remain in the middle of geopolitical turmoil working down munitions stockpiles amongst other areas, DoW continues to have interests aligned with higher volume output, Q3 is the cleanest quarter across the board we can remember – LMT GD NOC LHX RTX – nothing is perfect but Q3 was as close as we’ve seen in recent memory. The path on the budget appears, with some noise, likely higher not lower over the short and medium term.

In short: stockpiles are being run down faster than they can be rebuilt, the Department of War wants more volume, the third quarter was about as clean as the primes ever get, and the desk sees the budget drifting higher despite the noise, with L3Harris (LHX) and RTX (RTX) the names it highlights. So Goldman says the budget goes up, TD Cowen says it goes flat, and Capital Alpha says to stop staring at this year's budget and ask who the Gulf buys from in 2030.

Meanwhile, the Treasury has already cast its vote. As we showed in our breakdown of the worst October budget deficit on record, US national defense outlays did something we still can’t quite explain: they hit $128.9 billion in a single month, blowing past every prior peak, none of which had cleared much more than $100 billion. Somebody is paying to refill those interceptor racks, and maybe this is what it looks like.

Which makes the flat-versus-higher topline debate look a little quaint: the checks are going out before Congress has decided anything.

There is one scenario where all three agree, at least implicitly. As Callan notes, a nuclear strike would probably hurt the defense budget and export orders alike. It would be the rare case where the biggest bomb in the inventory is bearish for the people who make bombs.

Maybe They Do, Maybe They Don't

Callan concedes up front that he cannot pin down consensus because it changes daily, with the market leaning toward post-election strikes one week and a settlement the next. JPMorgan's commodity desk calls it a coin flip. Goldman's Privorotsky expects the escalation premium back by Thursday. And the president says the war ends "fairly soon," as he has, give or take, since March.

If we have to pick a side (and we do), it is with the skeptics on all three counts. Air power alone will not bring down the Islamic Republic, so any closing strike is a performance. The performance most likely to be staged is a conventional one on Pickaxe, sometime after the next round of talks stalls, since it is the only item on the menu that lets everyone declare victory. And the nuclear version stays where Callan puts it: remote, self-defeating, and impossible to dismiss entirely with carriers in theater and iodine tablets going door to door.

In the meantime, the interceptors keep getting fired, the tankers keep burning and the bypass pipelines keep getting hit, whatever the S&P thinks on any given Monday.

more in the full Capital Alpha note "Lots of Variables in Resumption of Middle East War. The Nuke Question.", Goldman's "GS Basics" and "A&D from here" desk notes and the JPMorgan Market Intelligence morning briefing, all available to pro subs.

items.title: Would-Be Trump Assassin Ryan Routh Files 178-Page Appeal, Blames Trump-Appointed Judge
items.content_text:
Would-Be Trump Assassin Ryan Routh Files 178-Page Appeal, Blames Trump-Appointed Judge

Authored by Ken Silva via Headline USA,

Would-be Trump assassin Ryan Routh filed a 178-page appeal on Monday, asking to have his conviction overturned on the grounds that he didn't receive a fair trial.

Routh was the man found hiding in some bushes at Trump's golf course on Sept. 15, 2024. As Trump was golfing on another hole, a Secret Service agent spotted Routh pointing a rifle at the agent. The agent shot at Routh six times from about five feet away - missing all his shots and causing the would-be assassin to flee the scene. He was caught about 45 minutes later on the I-95 in Martin County. He was arrested, found guilty earlier this year of attempting to assassinate Trump, and sentenced to life in prison.

But according to his appeal, he never received a fair trial.

For starters, the presiding judge was Aileen Cannon, who was appointed by Trump, refused to recuse herself. Cannon also cut Routh's opening and closing statements short, and denied him access to classified information that the government holds about him.

NEW: Would-be Trump assassin Ryan Routh has filed a 178-page appeal against his conviction.
Perhaps the most interesting argument is that Judge Aileen Cannon improperly allowed the DOJ to withhold classified information from Routh. Cannon ruled that the disclosure of the... https://t.co/Qn0yFf9ziD pic.twitter.com/aHpFO5Etjz

— Ken Silva (@JD_Cashless) November 12, 2026

"In allowing the government to withhold discovery, the district court erred in failing to consider whether the information would be helpful to the defense. Instead, the court granted the motion based only on findings that the government made a sufficient showing that the information was classified and that its disclosure could cause serious damage or exceptionally grave damage to the national security of the United States," Routh's attorneys argued.

Routh is currently being held at the federal supermax prison in Florence, Colorado - the home of Oklahoma City bombing accomplice Terry Nichols, World Trade Center attacker Ramsey Yousef, and other terrorists.

The DOJ has yet to respond to his appeal.
