To put the question another way: What deeper mindset will Democrats take into these battles? Will they approach the next year as if we’re still locked in a deep crisis—as if the constitutional order still hangs in the balance, requiring maximal exercises of power? Or will they enter with a more lax posture, as though their midterm victory has brought things more or less under control, and the crisis has largely been averted?

“We’ll still be facing a lawless president,” Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland told us. While Van Hollen stressed that this would only be one piece of the Democratic agenda, he added: “And that will require complete pushback.”

“We’ll still be facing a lawless president.... And that will require complete pushback.”
–Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland

But, unfortunately, not all Democrats see things in these crisis-like terms. And it’s unclear whether the ones who do will be willing to act accordingly, or will be able to persuade their reluctant colleagues to rise to the moment and be sufficiently confrontational.

Every Democrat we spoke with agreed that the Trump administration is world-historically corrupt, and most expected his lawbreaking to persist or even escalate. Some do seem willing to contemplate suspension of the regular order of things, if that’s what it takes to slow or stop the lawlessness. Others, though, seem more resigned to running a playbook for normal times, one that’s plainly unsuited to the coming moment.


Checks and Balances? Under Trump?

To obstruct, all Trump has to do is say no. No, we will not cooperate with your investigations. No, we will not prosecute people who defy your subpoenas. No, we will not follow the law.

The key to understanding the dilemma Democrats now face is that our system of checks and balances rests on a shared baseline commitment to upholding the rule of law. Trump is the first president of the modern era to openly dispense with the notion that justice should be blind, and to declare the Constitution as nonbinding on his tribune-like powers. Trump feels exactly zero responsibility to act as steward of the constitutional order or preserve it for future generations. So the coming period of divided government could devolve into tests of will and raw power. Those, in turn, risk toppling us quickly into crisis. And the deeper problem is that when good guys blink, or appease transgressors, they don’t just end the acute crisis of the moment. They consign us all to new precedents. New double standards. New depths of doubt that a fair and just democracy can be restored.

Every Democrat we spoke to anticipates the very worst from Trump. They expect intense obstruction. Noncompliance with oversight requests and demands. Refusal to be bound by the strings attached to money, which the Constitution entrusts Congress to shell out and control. And a bottomless willingness to drag things out in court, with the undisguised goal of nullifying controversies by tying them up for months or years—perhaps even until this administration is over and the controversies are moot.

Normal checks and balances don’t have great answers to this.

In modern practice, Congress has leaned heavily on a standard set of tools for conducting oversight and seeking accountability. Committees request documents and testimony. Aides and members work behind the scenes to understand the often-opaque inner workings of the government. When they hit roadblocks, they demand depositions and further production of evidence. If the administration resists, they issue subpoenas. If officials flout their subpoenas, they can be held in contempt of Congress, at the risk of civil and criminal penalties, including big fines and even arrest and hard prison time.

These tools can be quite effective, even in adversarial conflict with an executive branch controlled by the other party. The oil that keeps it all functioning is a basic willingness, however reluctant, to preserve our system of government. This generally means officials don’t ignore their subpoenas sight unseen, they agree to appear at congressional hearings, and they don’t treat public money as theirs to spend or dole out to friends and allies.

When those assumptions no longer apply—and they certainly do not apply with Trump—Congress quickly runs out of normal tools to enforce compliance, and the majority has to choose: resign itself to being spat upon, or embrace significantly more aggressive tactics.

Josh Chafetz, a legal scholar at Georgetown who wrote the definitive book about Congress’s hidden tools, notes that the Democratic majority in the House struggled to respond to Trump’s obstruction of oversight in 2019 and 2020. The first Trump administration was historically contemptuous of congressional prerogatives, but it still honored some norms—for example, officials did attend hearings, and agencies did occasionally cooperate with oversight requests. Now things are likely to get more confrontational—much more so.

“The Democrats in the last two years of the first Trump administration sort of ran up against some of the limits,” Chafetz said. “Now they’re going to run up against those limits even harder.”


How Democrats Can Bring Down the Hammer—If They So Choose

So what would it look like if Democrats were to deploy maximal power against the administration next year? To escalate, Democrats would likely have to test one or all of the following approaches:

• Inherent contempt, a rarely invoked mechanism that allows Congress to imprison or otherwise penalize people who defy lawful commands.

• Impeachment, which threatens executive branch officials with the prospect of removal and places Congress at the height of its constitutional authority.

• The power of the purse, which allows Congress to place conditions on the money it authorizes the government to spend.

Unfortunately, as we learned in our conversations with lawmakers and aides, many Democrats are inclined to disclaim some of these methods.

That isn’t entirely a sign of weakness. Congress has not invoked its inherent contempt authority in almost 100 years, in part because it’s rarely been necessary, and in part because it’s messy.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed that the Constitution empowers Congress to enforce its own will; if a reluctant witness refuses to testify, Congress can punish him directly. In recent years, when members have flirted with inherent contempt, they’ve toyed with the idea of imposing fines on contemptuous witnesses.

But historically, Congress would dispatch its sergeant at arms and other law enforcement officers that he or she might deputize to arrest and detain those witnesses. For obvious reasons, this is thorny: If the witness is a member of the executive branch, with an executive branch security detail, what happens in an armed standoff?

“I have discussed inherent contempt with leadership and some of the oversight committee chairs.”
–Representative Ted Lieu, a member of the incoming House Democratic leadership team

This tactic is being debated at high levels among Democrats, according to Representative Ted Lieu, a member of the incoming House Democratic leadership team. “I have discussed inherent contempt with leadership and some of the oversight committee chairs,” Lieu told us. Still, he cautioned, any such move would be litigated, just like more standard processes. And we are skeptical that the idea has much traction among other Democrats. As one senior Senate aide told us, inherent contempt is “really fun to talk about,” but because it seems politically onerous, radical, and difficult to implement, it’s a “long shot.”

Impeachment, by contrast, should be much less controversial, and can be very effective at speeding up investigations and prying information loose. That’s in part because courts will be more deferential to an impeachment inquiry than to congressional committees conducting normal oversight. Witnesses also feel especially compelled to cooperate and are uniquely protected if they do. In 2019, investigators in the Democratic-controlled House were mostly stymied—until Trump’s first impeachment, at which point administration officials came out of the woodwork to testify in astounding detail about his corrupt scheme to pressure Ukraine to subvert the 2020 election.

This is why we think Democrats should be prepared to deploy the impeachment power promiscuously—including against Trump’s most controversial Cabinet officials. To give just one example, they should seriously contemplate impeaching Attorney General Todd Blanche for his corrupt prosecutions of Trump critics and for concealing important chunks of the Epstein files. This would be justified on the merits, but it would also maximize Congress’s investigative power over the Justice Department, where all sorts of malfeasance surely remains hidden from view.

But to do all this, Democrats would have to be overwhelmingly united. And as of this writing, they plainly are not. As Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois recently pleaded: “Don’t be impeaching anybody. Let’s just get back to work, and maybe we can come to compromises.”

“I know [impeachment proceedings] will be very difficult for a lot of my colleagues. But Trump has simply become so dangerous that it needs to be done.”
–Representative Adam Smith, a moderate from Washington state who’s the incoming Armed Services Committee chair

Representative Adam Smith, a moderate from Washington state who’s the incoming Armed Services Committee chair, backs impeaching Trump. Smith told us he anticipated that Democrats from swingy or red districts and states will be reluctant to support impeachment proceedings. “I know this will be very difficult for a lot of my colleagues,” Smith said. “But Trump has simply become so dangerous that it needs to be done.”


Coming Soon: The Democrats’ First Test

Which leaves the spending power. If inherent contempt and impeachment remain off the table, congressional budget authority will be Democrats’ only real power tool, and they’ll have to wield it aggressively: no money for agencies that obstruct investigations. No money for key Justice Department offices so long as they’re withholding the Epstein files or corruptly prosecuting Trump critics. No money for the illegal war against Iran or illegal executions of supposed drug smugglers on the high seas. And so on.

In the decades since Congress cut off funding for the Vietnam War, however, Republicans have been much more inclined than Democrats to wield this power in divided government—with one notable exception.

Last year, when Obamacare subsidies were on the verge of expiring, Democrats withheld their votes to fund the government, contingent on the demand that Congress extend those tax credits. Republicans refused, and appropriations lapsed. The government furloughed federal workers across agencies, impacting everything from air travel to IRS assistance to environmental cleanup projects. And here’s the kicker: Even though the Democrats could fairly be said to have caused the shutdown in the immediate sense, Republicans shouldered more of the blame. Democrats were wielding power and doing so effectively. Then, abruptly, a bloc of Senate Democrats decided they’d made their point. They folded a winning hand, and the shutdown ended.

To vindicate their power of the purse, Democrats in this coming Congress will have to show greater stamina and resolve. Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut argues that it actually undermines the Democratic Party’s core complaints about Trump—that his authoritarianism is a threat to the republic—when Democrats are unwilling to deploy this power against those things. “I do not think it helped our messaging over the last year and a half that we broadly weren’t willing to deny them funding for departments that were operating clearly outside of the bounds of the law,” Murphy told us.

The first test of Democratic mettle will arrive much more quickly than you might think. In December, almost a full month before Democrats reclaim power, the current operating budget for the federal government will expire. Democrats could insist on defunding the Iran war straight away. But at the very least, they should agree to only a very brief extension of funding. This would prevent the government from shutting down over the holidays, which would surely be unpopular. But more to the point, a short extension would allow Democrats to preserve their leverage over Trump, because the budget would have to be renegotiated in early 2027. Trump and Republicans will want a longer-term extension for precisely this reason. And that could escalate into a standoff.

Most Democrats we talked to expect the party to dig in. “We’re going to be confronted very quickly with a decision as to whether we’re going to use appropriations as leverage,” Murphy said, adding that effective oversight will be impossible if Democrats refuse to hold the line.

“I hope we will use our appropriations power as a hammer against any further political persecutions of American citizens.”
–Jamie Raskin, incoming chair of the Judiciary Committee

“My view,” Van Hollen added, “is either Republicans work with us to begin to make changes that we think are necessary, or, yes, we have a short-term [budget] punting it into the beginning of next year.”

More broadly, for this method to work—for it to end the Iran war, rein in ICE, end Trump’s vindictive prosecutions, and secure the release of the Epstein files—Democrats would have to resolve themselves to potentially leaving large parts of the government unfunded, in ways that they find politically challenging.

Some Democrats do appear prepared to refuse funding, even if it results in protracted standoffs, to accomplish things like thwarting Trump’s corrupt prosecutions. “I hope we will use our appropriations power as a hammer against any further illegitimate political persecutions of American citizens for their political speech,” Jamie Raskin, incoming chair of the Judiciary Committee, told us, stressing he will make this case to appropriators.

Representative Yassamin Ansari, a member of the Oversight Committee, agreed. “The Trump administration is using taxpayer resources to attack the president’s perceived enemies,” Ansari said. “We must stop funneling taxpayer dollars into Trump’s agencies that abuse their power and violate Americans’ rights.”

“We must stop funneling taxpayer dollars into Trump’s agencies that abuse their power and violate Americans’ rights.”
–Representative Yassamin Ansari, a member of the Oversight Committee

Murphy, who is an informal leader of a similarly stalwart faction in the Senate, is ready for long struggles, too. He says Democrats should hold up Defense Department spending entirely to force an end to the Iran war. “I think it would be a pretty popular move for us to draw a hard line and say, ‘We are willing to fund the military, but only if this war ends,’” Murphy told us. “It would force Republicans and the administration into spending more time and oxygen defending the war.”

But Murphy readily allows that he can’t force that dilemma on Republicans unless the Senate Democratic caucus is with him. “I think there will be a question,” he acknowledged carefully, “as to whether Democrats are willing … to hold up the entirety of the defense budget over a commitment to end the war.”


Affordability vs. Accountability: A False Choice

We see another problem lurking in the Democratic mindset. Some Democrats have taken to arguing that the threshold test for the party’s agenda—legislative or oversight—should be a simple one: Does it improve the lives of ordinary people? Yes, or no?

We’re not disputing that members of Congress are elected to deliver benefits to their constituents—to make people’s lives better. Obviously, they must pass such measures, even if Trump vetoes them. But there’s a problem with formulating this standard as a hard-and-fast rule: It creates a back door for some Democrats to avoid doing difficult things in defense of the rule of law, in defense of immigrants or other marginalized groups, even in defense of their own powers as leaders of a coequal branch.

There will quickly come a point when House Democrats must decide whether to take politically difficult stances on things that aren’t obviously connected to the immediate material circumstances of their constituents. If, for instance, Trump orders the DOJ to prosecute more of his critics, and Democrats confront whether to withhold funding from that office to end another outbreak of lawlessness, would that tangibly make ordinary people’s lives better? What about the debate over how to rein in Trump’s mass-deportation regime and his lawless ICE agents? Democrats will want, at a minimum, to draw hard lines against things like ICE’s warrantless searches, ICE’s mask-wearing, and Customs and Border Patrol—which has been responsible for a great deal of brutality—operating in the country’s interior. Some Democrats, at least, hope to use government funding as a lever to force an end to those things. Would that improve ordinary people’s lives, or not?

This mindset, we fear, will create additional cover for Democrats who are already inclined to avoid confrontation for other reasons. When very difficult political choices arise—over, say, whether to defund offices within DOJ to derail a corrupt prosecution—those Democrats will argue that their election victory was about “affordability,” and that defunding DOJ will do nothing to ease voters’ kitchen-table concerns.

Party strategists and a subset of commentators will no doubt agree. But Democrats should think hard right now about what such a surrender would look like after millions and millions of voters handed them an array of powers and authorities to check a lawless authoritarian president.

We’re arguing for this not just because we think our approach has more merit in the abstract. It’s also that the supposed tension between cost-of-living issues and accountability is mostly fictitious.

Consider, first, that there’s very little chance Trump will sign legislation that Democrats pass to ease cost-of-living concerns. He has shown no appetite for signing measures that redound to the political benefit of Democrats. And so, practically speaking, if kitchen-table issues crowd out accountability measures, Democrats will be choosing to focus on symbolic advances—cost-of-living legislation that Trump vetoes—over doing things where their power actually can slow or stop Trump.

Second, there is no fixed budget for congressional priorities. Democrats can do many things at once. Joe Biden signed the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022, just days after the last substantive hearing of the House January 6 Committee in late July. Why can’t this incoming Congress impeach Pete Hegseth one day and send Trump a bill restoring Medicaid coverage the next? Of course it can.

“If we want this government to work for the people, then we have to put an end to corruption and restore the rule of law.”
–Virginia Representative James Walkinshaw, a prominent member of the moderate New Democrat caucus

We also think that, in the minds of voters, when the economy is stagnant and the president is looting the country for personal gain, there is no clear distinction between anti-corruption politics and pocketbook politics. Exposing, ending, and punishing corruption will make economic life in America fairer by definition. And that will place Democrats on the side of the people who play by the rules.

Framed in this way, anti-corruption politics can unite the caucus and avoid the divisions that flow from establishing a false choice between kitchen-table concerns and checks and balances.

Some Democrats appear to agree with us. “If we want this government to work for the people, then we have to put an end to corruption and restore the rule of law,” Virginia Representative James Walkinshaw, a prominent member of the moderate New Democrat caucus, told us. “I don’t think there’s any conflict between being substantively centrist or pragmatic [and] recognizing that Congress has a responsibility to assert its constitutional role. I don’t think those two things are in tension.”


Going After the Abettors

None of this is to say conventional oversight tools indicate weakness in and of themselves. These tools have their place, and they can function as intended, even against a lawless president like Trump. They did in his first term, and they surely will again.

After all, it was Michael Cohen’s 2019 testimony to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, obtained during a standard congressional hearing, that established the basis for New York Attorney General Letitia James’s sprawling lawsuit against the Trump organization.

Trump may rage and sputter. He may test our ability to imagine the outer limits of “high crimes and misdemeanors.” But he is also entering his lame-duck years a loser. He will become a more diminished figure, whose power to bully elites and underlings into line will ebb. Congressional aides tell us they expect some administration officials to grow more willing to appear before Congress—if not to turn over documents—as Trump weakens. If they’re right, this will create more incriminating moments, as when Cohen testified nearly eight years ago.

Aides also expect the pace of whistleblowing to pick up. The protections that a congressional majority can offer will render people “more willing to come forward,” one aide told us, adding that recent conversations she’s had with would-be whistleblowers left her persuaded that “there are a lot of people who have stories to share.” After the country rejected Trump so overwhelmingly, their willingness to speak out is likely to grow.

Civil contempt is another option. This mechanism outsources subpoena enforcement to judges, who can levy fines on noncompliant officials. It avoids the obvious problems associated with inherent contempt, though it operates at a much slower pace. And it’s very plausible that officials will grow less willing to risk a big financial hit on behalf of a sunsetting Trump, particularly with many in his party looking beyond him.

“In theory, you could have an individual fined on a daily, weekly, or monthly basis for the time that they’re not complying with a subpoena,” Walkinshaw tells us. “We absolutely have to be willing to do that.”

Also in this bucket: private-sector actors who abetted Trump’s corruption. Multiple Democrats privately told us that they will be looking for creative ways to bring oversight to bear on entities—law firms, media companies, universities—that capitulated to pressure to make “deals” that in effect handed money or resources to Trump’s pet causes. Other Democrats are already discussing oversight of corporations that handed thinly veiled bribes to Trump in the form of “donations” to his imperial projects and campaign committees and were rewarded with favorable treatment from the government, such as the companies that received government contracts after donating to Trump’s ballroom.

The key nuance here is that this creates a route to direct oversight of Trump’s corruption that he can’t obstruct. These entities can’t simply defy oversight demands without creating serious legal and financial risk for themselves. With Democrats taking power, Trump in decline, and the public clearly arrayed against him, incentives will align for executives to divulge internal communications about their decision to bandwagon with Trump’s corruption.

“By focusing on outside actors, you have a better chance of getting information,” a senior Senate aide told us. Yet some Democrats are already balking at this approach: One bafflingly told Politico that such oversight would constitute “banana republic” conduct, when in fact it would be about undoing Trump’s efforts to turn us into a banana republic.

These entities will plead that they only surrendered to Trump under duress. But caving was optional. Every company and firm and university that held to principle survived—even flourished. As for those that didn’t, to the extent that they want to contend they played ball with Trump’s corrupt schemes only because they felt they had no choice, Democrats should confront them with a new demand: that they show meaningful public support for new anti-corruption legislation to set things right.

Finally, there’s the simple tactic of gathering information that might be usable for future prosecutions if Democrats win the presidency in 2028 and a real attorney general takes over. That becomes germane if Congress is able to discover clear violations of federal law—actual, legitimate violations, as opposed to the fake ones drummed up by Trump’s DOJ—on the part of Trump officials or outside actors who corruptly collaborated with them. Indeed, Lieu told us he intends to question witnesses with this in mind. “One of the main things we should do is get evidence for the next Department of Justice,” Lieu said, adding that such evidence could also be grist for prosecutions by state attorneys general.

As Ocasio-Cortez proved, this can work under careful questioning of cooperative witnesses. But it works by delegating and deferring accountability. The damage Trump can do in the meantime—to immigrants, to alliances, to our constitutional system—will be incalculable.


A Fight Caucus

One of the frustrating things about this lack of consensus among Democrats right now is that past congresses have shown more mettle in less perilous times.

The House impeached Andrew Johnson for improperly firing a Cabinet official, and while that was controversial, it’s a reminder that impeachment should remain a tool when serious circumstances warrant it. In 1879, the House of Representatives arrested a U.S. envoy to China—an executive branch official—for the comparably small sin of concealing official ledgers, which Congress believed might show evidence of waste or theft. Why should this approach be verboten when Congress has so many more pressing affronts to its authority to beat back?

Some outside voices are starting to make the case for hardball tactics like inherent contempt. “I do not think that’s a dead end,” Georgetown’s Chafetz said. He asked us to envision a scenario in which Congress detains Elon Musk, who enjoys extraordinarily lucrative government contracts, for refusing to testify about his conversations with Trump about their quid pro quo corruption. Trump would undoubtedly claim executive privilege applies, and his claim would be litigated in court—possibly for months or years. Meanwhile, Musk could plead with the courts to order his release—but while those cases are pending, he’d be stuck in some kind of holding facility. “It doesn’t seem particularly outlandish for a private citizen who is defying a congressional subpoena to be held in custody while that defiance is litigated,” Chafetz told us.

In the end, we think that Democrats who resist this sort of approach will be susceptible to a combination of factors: public pressure, Trump’s escalating lawlessness, and cajoling from more energetic peers. Leaders who believe we’re still in the midst of crisis, and who feel pained when Democrats shrink from challenges, should prod reluctant colleagues to join them.

Indeed, we think these energetic Democrats should formally organize for what’s coming by creating Fight Caucuses—one in the House, one in the Senate. Large blocs of members in the Freedom Caucus, Progressive Caucus, Blue Dog Coalition, and other caucuses routinely bring influence to bear that changes the strategic direction of whole parties.

A Fight Caucus in the House could do the same. It can demand enforceable concessions from Jeffries, who will want a free and easy path to the speakership. We similarly hope that outside advocacy groups—existing ones, or new ones—will treat constitutional hardball as a litmus test that Democrats must meet, no less than support for abortion rights, universal health care, or environmental protection. They can give each member a Fight Score, and provide direction to Democratic Party primary voters: This candidate was a stalwart fighter for democracy, constitutional governance, and the rule of law. That candidate was not.

Ansari, for her part, says she’s open to the idea of Fight Caucuses. And she makes a critical point: Organizing within the caucuses in defense of the rule of law could improve party cohesion. “It’s a great way to unify people,” Ansari said, noting that “fighting corruption and authoritarianism” has adherents in “every part of the caucus.”

Perhaps the best message for hesitant Democrats is to remind them of who Trump is. He is incorrigible. Much as some may want to proceed as if everything’s normal, he will leave them no choice. All they do by resisting confrontation is let him set the terms on which inevitable power struggles unfold.

We are entering a period that will be defined by a paradox. On one hand, Trump will take his abuses of power and assaults on the constitutional order to dangerous new lows. On the other hand, in the eyes of the public—and even in the eyes of many in his own party—he will be seen as a naked and exposed tyrant, an increasingly ludicrous figure who’s passing from the political scene. The best way to resolve this paradox is for Democrats to mount a full-on offensive to save the country. The emergency remains; but the despot’s attempt to cement authoritarian rule has been dealt a potentially fatal setback. Now is the time to bury this national nightmare once and for all, by deploying every last shred of congressional power to that end.

items.title: MAGA Fury Erupts as Trump Blurts Out Damning Admission about GOP Loss
items.content_text: In an interview with CBS News, Donald Trump acknowledged that a big reason for the GOP electoral bloodbath was his mass deportations. In one sense, this is absurd, given his elevation of Stephen Miller to chief of staff. But in another sense, Trump did admit to things in the interview that are anathema to MAGA: that undocumented immigrants are good workers, and that Americans think immigration is good for our country. MAGA erupted wildly over this. One influencer raged that if Trump does amnesty, “I’m done.” Another insisted that this would be a “disaster.” Still another fumed: “WITHOUT DEPORTATIONS, OUR COUNTRY IS GONE.” We sorted through all this with political scientist Julia Azari, who’s been writing well on this election for the “Good Politics/Bad Politics” Substack. We discuss what Trump revealed about the MAGA coalition’s crackup, the deeper forces driving it, why JD Vance will struggle to knit it back together, and how Democrats can drive wedges deep into it going forward. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: Statue Mocking Trump’s Draft Dodging Pops Up After Election Defeat
items.content_text:
Another statue commemorating Donald Trump’s mediocrity has appeared in Washington, this time mocking the moment he evaded the Vietnam War draft with a timely diagnosis of bone spurs.

The bronze installment—erected by an anonymous artist collective on the National Mall—is titled The Foot Soldier, and depicts the president sitting on a pedestal as he rubs his bare foot.

“We honor the service and sacrifice of our commander in chief, Donald J. Trump,” reads a plaque just underneath the guerilla monument. “He’s a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs.”

“We salute a leader who knows you can’t spell sacrifice without ‘I,’ and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you’re called to stand up, it’s best to just sit down and rest your feet,” the plaque concludes, before inscribing a quote from America’s fastidious and battle-worn leader: “‘I can be very military.’ —President Donald J. Trump.”

It’s not the first time that Trump has been immortalized by his critics. Another bronze emulation of the president materialized on the National Mall just last year, portraying Trump in a gleeful handshake with his former “best friend,” child sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. The statue was named Why Can’t We Be Friends? and was accompanied by a similarly designed plaque that displayed four lines of poetry Trump wrote Epstein for the criminal financier’s fiftieth birthday.

That version was created by the incognito collective The Secret Handshake, and managed to stay on the mall for several months.

A golden incarnation of the president, titled King of the World, also popped up earlier this year, showcasing Trump embracing Epstein a la the famous scene from Titanic in which Jack holds Rose as she stretches out her arms at the bow of the ship.

“The tragic love story between Jack and Rose was built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches,” the statue’s plaque read at the time. “This monument honors the bond between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein, a friendship seemingly built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches.”

items.title: Trump Obsesses Over Dana White After He Refuses to Join White House
items.content_text:
President Trump appears to be doubling down on trying to get Ultimate Fighting Championship President and CEO Dana White to be White House press secretary.

Trump posted multiple artificial intelligence–generated videos of White on Truth Social Monday afternoon, including one where music plays as White triumphantly assumes the role to cheering crowds and another where he berates a reporter in a crowded press room.

The posts contradict Trump’s claim Sunday that the job offer was just a joke.

“I will tell you, I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea, and there’s only one Dana. He’s great,” Trump said to reporters in Palm Beach.

On Saturday, Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that he was offering the press secretary position to White. “I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris,” Trump wrote. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

The UFC magnate reportedly declined the offer, and on social media, many users speculated that Trump meant to pick conservative Dana W. White, a former Pentagon spokesperson. But she said there was no mix-up.

“To everyone texting me congratulations: thank you, but you have the wrong Dana White. I’ve stood at the podium and taken questions from the Pentagon press corps. I have never stood in an octagon. I’d like to keep it that way,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

Meanwhile, the UFC chief flew to Washington to meet with Trump in the White House on Monday, meaning that the idea could be gaining steam. Why he would take the job is unclear, although he has a positive relationship with Trump and staged a UFC fight on the White House lawn for Trump’s birthday earlier this year.

items.title: Lauren Boebert Defeated by Blue Wave as Democrat Cruises to Victory
items.content_text:
Colorado MAGA Representative Lauren Boebert has been washed away in the blue wave, losing her election to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a stunning upset that is one of many GOP midterm failures.

Laubacher won with 48.77 percent of the vote, while Boebert had only secured 47.92 percent of the vote when CNN called the race.

Laubacher is a retired two-star United States Navy rear admiral who served on former President Joe Biden’s National Security Council.

Boebert’s tenure in Congress was extremely incendiary. She was a staunch supporter of President Trump and his election denial claims, and was a vocal supporter of the QAnon right-wing conspiracy theory community. She is opposed to the LGBTQ community as a whole, and often harassed Representative Sarah McBride, the first transgender member of Congress.

In 2023, Boebert and a male partner were kicked out of a showing of Beetlejuice for vaping, singing, filming, and groping one another. In September, she was the subject of a House ethics complaint for having physical and emotional relationships with three of her own staffers—chief of staff Jeffrey Small, district director Clarice Navarro, and district chief of staff Raven Finegan—and paying them to be quiet about it. Boebert denied the allegations.

items.title: MAGA Rep. Asked Trump Team to Intervene in Criminal Investigation
items.content_text:
Representative Andy Ogles’s legal team pleaded with the Trump administration to drop a probe into his campaign finances. Months later, the Justice Department complied.

Emails obtained by the nonprofit organization American Oversight and published Monday by RawStory revealed that Ogles’s attorneys reached out to the then-director of the DOJ’s Weaponization Working Group, Edward Martin, to end the investigation in November 2025.

“Please see the attached letter on behalf of our client, Rep. Andy Ogles, seeking the termination of the Department’s criminal investigation into campaign finance issues that are more appropriately addressed by the FEC and the House Ethics Committee,” the email read.

Two weeks later, after no response from Martin, Ogles’s legal team followed up to prompt a written response, this time cc-ing Jordan Fox, the chief of staff to then-deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche.

“Received. Thank you,” Martin responded, signing off as “Ed.”

Months later in May, the DOJ agreed to return Ogles’s cell phone back to the Tennessee lawmaker, signalling the end of the inquiry.

It is not clear if Martin followed through on escalating Ogles’s request to DOJ higher ups, or if the request was immediately tied to the end result. But it is an alarming indication of how backdoor favors are clearly expected, and how they operate, within the Trump administration, particularly for the president’s most loyal MAGA lapdogs.

The investigation was related to discrepancies in Ogles’s 2022 campaign finance records, when he filed a report claiming that he loaned his campaign $320,000. The detail raised alarm bells in 2024, when Ogles filed another campaign finance report to acknowledge that he had only loaned the campaign $20,000.

The following year, a U.S House Congressional Ethics panel found “substantial reason to believe” that Ogles had violated federal campaign finance laws by inflating his offices’ fundraising via a personal loan. The lawmaker’s legal defense torched the FBI’s decision to claim his phone, arguing that the bureau—as a component of the executive branch—had no right to look at the personal communications of a sitting member of the legislative branch.

“Members of Congress who are political allies of the incumbent president should not be able to evade prosecution by going through improper channels to request leniency or favoritism,” interim chief counsel at American Oversight Katherine M. Kennedy wrote to Inspector General Don R. Berthiaume last month, according to RawStory.

items.title: Thomas Massie Forces Vote on Impeaching Pete Hegseth
items.content_text:
Representative Thomas Massie presented eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Monday afternoon. 

Massie posted his draft resolution hours earlier on X with the message, “I’ve seen some of my colleagues say @SecWar Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they’ll vote not to impeach. That’s not the question though. The question is whether he committed impeachable acts, and the answer is yes, eight times.”

Those eight instances include three counts of waging war on Iran without congressional authorization; ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties; conducting extrajudicial killings with U.S. strikes on so-called “drug boats” in the Southern hemisphere; suppressing free speech by targeting Senator Mark Kelly’s criticism of U.S. military policy; the U.S. kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without constitutional or legal authority; and waging war on Yemen without congressional authorization. 

Hegseth seems to have lost support from Trump as well as other Republicans in Washington. Trump told Fox News on Sunday that Hegseth was “one of the guys that was most responsible” for the Iran war. On the same day, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that he is a “hard yes” for impeachment. 

“The so-called ‘secretary of defense’ has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe,” Jeffries said on ABC’s This Week. “Pete Hegseth has got to go.” 

House Speaker Mike Johnson tried to avert Hegseth’s impeachment for nearly two months, canceling votes in September until after the midterm elections because he didn’t have enough votes to defeat the vote. Massie’s resolution at the time was privileged, and had Johnson not dismissed the House early, it would have been voted on within two days. 

“If Trump’s going to replace appointees like Hegseth, he should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate,” Massie wrote on X Thursday.  “Also, my Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials.”

Massie said last Wednesday that Hegseth could avert the vote if he resigned. That may be Hegseth’s plan, as he has called a press conference at the Pentagon Tuesday. He is rumored to be seeking an appointment to Tennessee’s open Senate seat, although Tennessee Governor-elect Marsha Blackburn has reportedly ruled that out.

items.title: Chuck Schumer’s Time May Be Up as Van Hollen Suddenly Pivots
items.content_text:
Senator Chris Van Hollen is open to running for Senate majority leader, amid mounting calls for Senator Chuck Schumer to pass the torch.

Van Hollen has “received an outpouring of calls and is now in active listening mode,” a person familiar with the Maryland Democrat’s thinking told Politico’s Playbook Monday.

“The door is not shut,” the person added.

Speaking to Fox 5 last week, Van Hollen indicated that he was interested in pursuing a higher office—but not the one people are begging him to take. “I’ve made clear that I’m not looking to be the next Democratic leader,” Van Hollen said. “I’ve been kicking the tires on a 2028 presidential election.”

But the Marylander declined to commit his support to Schumer, who has led the Democrats in the Senate since 2017.

“I think it’s important that the Senate Democratic Caucus have a full and open debate before we select the next leader, whoever that may be. I don’t think it should be automatic. And I think we need to have a plan, and we need to make it clear we’re going to be united by a common plan,” Van Hollen said.

He doubled down on his comments over the weekend, arguing that “nobody should get a blank check” without a greater discussion in the Democratic caucus.

Van Hollen has emerged as a leading progressive, after he traveled to El Salvador when his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García was illegally deported to a foreign gulag.

Van Hollen wasn’t the only Democratic senator who held back on supporting Schumer: Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut also declined to endorse the longtime caucus leader.

At the same time, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has publicly endorsed Van Hollen for the top post. “If he decides he wants to be Senate majority leader, I think he’d be amazing at the job,” El-Sayed told CNN last week.

items.title: Trump Blurts Out Surprise Admission About Losses, Wrecking MAGA’s Spin
items.content_text:
Everybody has had a good chuckle over Donald Trump’s new admission—delivered in an interview with CBS News—that his immigration agenda helped cause last week’s GOP electoral bloodbath. And for good reason: It comes right after Trump installed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, rewarding the architect of that agenda with even more prestige and power.

Yet as absurd as it is, Trump’s acknowledgment is still significant. Here’s why: It sabotages the preferred immigration-related explanation for the defeat that MAGA figures are offering to forestall any GOP softening on the issue. It undercuts JD Vance’s interpretation of the outcome too.

Trump’s admission came after CBS’s Ross Douthat asked if immigration had “hurt” in the midterms. “I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said. He claimed his sealing of the border was a political positive. But it “hurt,” Trump continued, that he deported “people with good jobs” who had committed only the “one violation” of originally entering the country illegally:

His midterms ass whoopin has Trump sounding almost woke on immigration https://t.co/g1msCV6I8B

— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 9, 2026

Notably, Trump also acknowledged that “a large group” of Americans think such immigrants “should be allowed to stay.” He added that for this group, the deportations might have been “too tough.”

The careful listener will grasp that Trump didn’t merely claim the deportation tactics themselves—the masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement snatchings, the paramilitary invasions of U.S. cities, the summary executions of innocent people on American streets—were the problem. He took it a step further, admitting that many Americans don’t think this class of immigrants should be removed at all, whatever tactics are deployed to do so.

To put it mildly, this is not the interpretation of the election that leading MAGA figures have adopted. Many have blamed the outcome largely on Trump’s Iran war and adopted other tricks to absolve all that niggling white nationalist stuff of any role in this catastrophe.

Let’s start with Vance. In his much-discussed tweet blaming the war for the GOP loss, Vance also slipped in a diagnosis of immigration’s role. “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement,” he said. This has been widely interpreted as a genuine concession. But it isn’t one.

After all, Vance also said that any “establishment politicians who say the solution to our woes is amnesty” is “lying to you.” So Vance merely allowed that enforcement tactics alienated voters. He’s not even entertaining the idea that voters also rebelled against the underlying ideological goal of ridding the country of immigrants whose only crime was to come here illegally in search of a better life.

Other MAGA figures have not only refused to entertain that notion—they’ve redoubled their rejection of it. As The Bulwark’s Will Sommer points out, some went as far as blaming immigration and nonwhite diversity in Texas for the GOP’s wipeout there. Others, like Laura Loomer, flatly declared that the overall results should only intensify MAGA’s commitment to ridding the country of immigrants and making it whiter again. The Atlantic’s Adam Serwer acidly notes that to these figures, the election only underscored that our real problem is that recent immigrants and their descendants get to vote at all.

Meanwhile, several Trumpist political operatives just launched a group called American Ascent, which will recruit young people to seek office on a hard-core “America First” platform. It’s partly founded on the idea that Trump’s mass deportations remain a political winner for the GOP and a major motivator of young voters, so Republicans must not back off from them.

To make this case, many of these MAGA figures have been cherry-picking from exit polls to supposedly show that America sided with them on mass deportations. They keep highlighting a finding that Republicans won very narrowly among voters who say immigration enforcement was “crucial” to their vote.

Yet the exit polls also show Democrats won a majority of those who said immigration enforcement was a “major” or “minor” (as opposed to “crucial”) factor. Republicans won only among the shriveled minority who accord extraordinary, overwhelming importance to the issue—the hard MAGA core.

In fact, the exit polls also show that 58 percent of voters said Trump’s enforcement has “gone too far.” And voters said immigrants “help the country,” rather than hurt, by 61 percent to 39 percent. If anything, Americans just ringingly endorsed racial and ethnic pluralism, as Shikha Dalmia writes, by electing people from a wide array of faiths and ethnicities all over the country.

In short: Most Americans think immigration is good. They believe enforcement has gone too far—not just with its violent tactics, but also with its underlying goal of emptying the country of immigrants.

There’s also the fact that Trump’s mass deportations helped drive high turnout and a swing back to Democrats among Latinos. It’s worth noting an amusing aside here: When Trump made huge gains among Latinos in 2024, MAGA-sympathetic pundits interpreted it as a sign that right-wing anti-immigrant nationalism could appeal to the nonwhite working class. Trumpism could appeal to Latino American citizens with deeper roots here and turn them against more recent arrivals, such as the alleged pet-eating Haitians in Ohio.

But now that Latinos have overwhelmingly snapped back to Democrats over Trump’s treatment of immigrants, MAGA figures have suddenly thrown away the idea that their ideology might appeal to that demographic. So, hey, let’s just deport them all instead!

In his own very limited way, Trump seems to have acknowledged on 60 Minutes that Americans like immigrants. Miller’s appointment means he won’t act on this realization. But his admission still undercuts the MAGA theory of this election, and of American politics more broadly, on a very deep level.

That’s because all these MAGA assessments—from Vance, from those explicit white nationalists, or from those operatives still committed to mass deportations—are linked by a common idea. It’s that these election results do not in any sense demonstrate a need to back off the project of ethnically cleansing the country and making it whiter and more Christian again.

In that telling, the election was not at all a rebuke to the MAGA vision of “heritage America,” the idea that those without deep ancestral and blood ties to the homeland should face expulsion to purify and restore the nation’s true identity. Those MAGA voices are wrong: This worldview, in addition to being based on bad history and terrible for the national interest, is a political fantasy. But to some still holed up in Fortress MAGA, the election results only confirm the deeper wisdom of it.

items.title: Pete Hegseth’s Future Looks Grim as Even Trump Starts to Turn on Him
items.content_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appears to be on the verge of getting kicked out of Washington.

Capitol Hill Republicans—including the president—have started to turn on Hegseth publicly. The bombastic former Fox News host could face a House impeachment vote as early as this week.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie originally introduced a 34-page impeachment resolution against the Defense secretary in mid-September, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors, and specifically of abusing the power of his office by advancing Donald Trump’s war against Iran without congressional approval.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz suggested that “one of the reasons the House has been out of session for a couple months is because they didn’t have the votes to stop a Hegseth impeachment” when Massie originally announced the articles. That has not changed.

Massie told MS NOW Monday that he planned to force a vote on the impeachment resolution that afternoon. Several members of the GOP believe it will pass.

But some conservatives are mulling over other solutions that could similarly strip Hegseth of his authority. Speaking with CNN’s Manu Raju Monday morning, retiring Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said it would be easier if Hegseth just resigned.

“I’m weighing it,” Bacon said when asked about the proposed articles of impeachment. “Eight articles, and I’m not very sympathetic to those articles.”

“But the areas that concern me most about the secretary aren’t in the articles of impeachment: firing and redlining abiding generals or admirals; withholding appropriated money all year from Ukraine,” Bacon said. “I’m not the only one that feels this way, there’s a bunch of us that have been talking about it.”

“Some of us don’t feel comfortable with [Massie’s] justifications,” Bacon added, describing Massie’s approach as libertarian, “but I think there are other ones out there.”

Even Trump blamed Hegseth for the Iran war, one of the main reasons Republicans lost so badly last week, while speaking to Fox News from West Palm Beach, Florida on Sunday. Trump claimed that the Pentagon chief was “one of the guys that was most responsible” for the conflict.

Exactly what becomes of the bombastic “secretary of war”—or his political future—after such an ousting is unclear.

Last week, Trump mused about the possibility of effectively pushing Hegseth into Tennessee’s open Senate seat. Trump told reporters Hegseth would be “very popular” as a replacement for Governor-elect Marsha Blackburn. The Hill reported that Hegseth had shown interest in the job, and was actively campaigning for it behind the scenes.

But that’s unlikely to happen: A source close to Blackburn told the Associated Press Thursday that Hegseth was not in consideration for the seat, and dismissed the ongoing rumors as “baseless chatter.”

items.title: Two More Top Officials Jump Ship After GOP Election Wipeout
items.content_text:
The Trump administration is hemorrhaging officials following Republicans’ crushing defeat in the midterm elections and Stephen Miller’s ascension to White House chief of staff. 

Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate resigned Monday, and White House deputy chief of staff Richard Walters handed in his resignation letter on Friday. That follows at least five other resignations of top officials in the Justice Department and the White House last week.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Shumate’s resignation in a post on X. “Under his leadership, the Division pursued important affirmative litigation to challenge sanctuary policies and delivered key wins in lawsuits against local policies that endangered federal law enforcement,” he wrote. “The Division also secured historic settlements to end illegal corporate DEI practices and shuttered dozens of clinics which were providing so-called ‘gender affirming care’ to minors. We are grateful for Brett’s service at DOJ and wish him continued success.” 

Shumate is the fourth DOJ official to resign in a week, following assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon quitting on Thursday as well as assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg and U.S. Attorney Jason Quiñones stepping down Friday. 

Walters, who resigned the same day as White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, told The Daily Beast in a statement that “Serving President Trump has been the honor of a lifetime and I will always be thankful to Susie Wiles for the opportunity.” He was Wiles’s deputy for only six months, after previously working as executive director for  President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance’s inaugural committee. 

“Stephen [Miller] is building an incredible and capable team to implement the President’s agenda and I look forward to being part of it from the outside,” Walters added. 

Miller told Fox News in a statement that “While he will be leaving us, Richard will continue to help from the outside as we continue to work with all of our strength to deliver for President Trump and his courageous fight to Save America.” 

Despite these conciliatory statements, it’s obvious that people are fleeing the Trump administration due to the rise of one its most reviled officials in Miller—and the likelihood of being hauled before a Democratic Congress as part of a wide-ranging investigation. The DOJ in particular is going to be in Democrats’ crosshairs, and nobody wants to spend the next two years having to lawyer up and avoid subpoenas.

items.title: Todd Blanche Loses His Mind Over Looming Democratic Investigations
items.content_text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche has completely lost the plot.

The Justice Department chief effectively confessed on CNN Sunday that the historically independent agency will investigate Democratic lawmakers at Donald Trump’s behest.

Leaning on their forthcoming congressional majority, Democratic lawmakers have advertised their intent to use oversight tools to investigate alleged misconduct and corruption in Trump’s MAGA administration. The president attempted to preempt the looming inspection over the weekend by likening it to a “criminal act,” which he ordered Blanche to investigate.

When explicitly asked by State of the Union host Dana Bash on Sunday whether he would comply with the president’s directive, Blanche flippantly accused Democrats of threatening “anybody that’s conservative and anybody that happens to be a Republican.”

“And over the last several days, we have seen the rhetoric even rise up, to the point where they’re already—before they’re even in power, they’re already talking about investigations and impeachments, with no basis, no facts, just out there running around,” Blanche claimed. “That should be something that President Trump is very concerned about, and certainly I am as well.”

But Blanche seemingly could not keep his cool after Bash brought up Congress’s constitutional duty to provide oversight. “Is that what you’re concerned about?” asked Bash.

“Wait. Hold on a second. Sorry,” Blanche responded. “Wait, wait, wait, wait. No, no, no, no, no. They have a very unique role in oversight. I agree. Have you been listening to the rhetoric the past couple days? You honestly think that all they’re doing is talking about their oversight obligations when they’re talking about going after basically every member of the Cabinet, they’re talking about impeachments, they’re talking about going after companies, private companies who happen to have made investments in this country over the past couple of years?”

“That is not oversight,” insisted the attorney general. “I welcome oversight. Oversight is exactly something they should be doing.”

But amidst Blanche’s sprawling rant, he failed to identify a single criminal act by the Democratic Party. In another portion of the interview, Blanche concurred that it was his duty as the DOJ chief to represent administration officials during impeachment proceedings.

Contrary to Blanche’s opinion, the Justice Department is supposed to be independent and free from presidential interference. That’s been true since at least Watergate, after which the agency established interdepartmental policies and new political norms to distance its operations from the White House.

But that started to shift in 2024, when the Supreme Court sided with Trump to expand his presidential immunity. At the time, Chief Justice John Roberts penned a majority decision that effectively transformed the Justice Department into an arm to be leveraged by the Oval Office, opening communication channels between the federal law enforcement agency and the presidency for all future investigations.

Since then, Trump has repeatedly used the Justice Department for his own personal gain, directing prosecutors to lead his retribution campaign, to investigate election records, and to strongarm other federal institutions.
